item.title: The U.S. Economy And Considerations For Monetary Policy, Federal Reserve Vice Chair For Supervision Michelle W. Bowman, At The C. Peter Mccolough Series On International Economics Council On Foreign Relations, Washington, D.C.
item.content:encoded:
Good afternoon. It is a pleasure to join you today at the Council on Foreign Relations to discuss my outlook for the U.S. economy.1

Economic growth has gained momentum this year, driven by robust investment demand and solid consumer spending, and the labor market now appears to have stabilized. These outcomes suggest that the policy rate cuts toward the end of last year helped to address some labor market weakness. We are experiencing rapid technological change and ongoing geopolitical tensions, while inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped and have shown recent signs of broadening. Despite these challenges, increased investment in and use of artificial intelligence (AI), or super intelligence, are boosting economic growth and productivity and American families appear to be resilient.

The Federal Reserve's monetary policy goals are to achieve maximum employment and price stability. While the labor market has improved more than I expected this year, our progress on lowering inflation has disappointed. Therefore, bringing inflation down remains a priority. I am also monitoring expectations about AI and energy prices, and how they influence the risks to achieving our mandates. Consistent with my views following our September FOMC meeting, I continue to focus on interpreting the underlying trends in the economy and the evolution of financial conditions.2

In my remarks today, I will review our most recent FOMC policy meeting and discuss current economic conditions and my near-term outlook for the economy. I will then turn to recent developments in energy markets and the AI buildout and will conclude with my thoughts on the appropriate path of monetary policy.

Update on the Most Recent FOMC Meeting
At last month's FOMC meeting, I joined my colleagues to support holding the federal funds rate target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent. This approach was consistent with my view that further changes in the policy rate should wait until we had a better understanding of how conditions would evolve and how the recent rate increase would influence the underlying trends in the economy. Maintaining the policy stance at the October meeting allowed us to assess the incoming data. While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated. It is also important to gain greater clarity on the effect of recent market volatility on financial conditions.

Economic and Financial Conditions
U.S. economic growth has stepped up this year. After rising a solid 2.4 percent during the first half of the year, real gross domestic product (GDP) likely increased at an even stronger pace of more than 3 percent in the third quarter, well above last year's 2 percent pace.3 Economic growth has been supported by robust increases in AI-related capital expenditures and solid consumer spending. However, some interest-rate-sensitive sectors like residential investment have declined, and the recent rise in mortgage rates appears to be dragging home construction and sales down further. Consumer spending has strengthened this year, despite softness in real incomes and declining sentiment, which are partly due to higher energy prices.

Labor Market Conditions
Labor market conditions look to have improved since last year. Over the course of this year, the unemployment rate has edged down to 4.1 percent in October, remaining close to my estimate of its natural rate. Job gains have been above last year's anemic pace, averaging about 80,000 per month through October, and have broadened across industries beyond health care and social assistance.

The labor market continues to show low dynamism, with low-hiring and low-firing conditions as we sometimes see in a late-cycle expansion. The job-finding rate has been low, especially for new labor force entrants, and the share of long-term unemployed workers has moved up significantly. Workers' perceptions of job availability in the Conference Board survey have remained soft in recent months. On their own, these data would be consistent with a higher unemployment rate than currently reported. However, layoffs have moved down this year, offsetting the softness in hiring. In plain terms, workers are both less likely to find a new job and less likely to be laid off, a somewhat unusual pattern.

Although stable, the labor market does not appear to be tight, as wage growth has slowed to a modest pace. On a 12-month basis, the wages and salaries component of the employment cost index increased 3.1 percent in September, the same pace as the change in average hourly earnings for October. Both measures have slowed noticeably from a year ago. An increasing number of workers have taken on a supplemental part-time job to make ends meet, as the share of multiple job holders has increased back to levels seen in early 2025. Given strong productivity gains in recent years, wage growth at this pace is in line with or even below the pace we would expect if inflation was running at 2 percent.

Inflation
Progress on lowering inflation has stalled over the past two years or so. Today's consumer price index suggests that 12-month core PCE inflation likely moved up further to 3.3 percent in October, as upward pressures from higher energy prices and AI-related demand continue to flow through to core goods and services prices.

Lack of progress on lowering inflation largely reflects a confluence of shocks unrelated to conditions in the labor market. Tariffs, energy, and AI-related price pressures each accounted for roughly one-fourth of above-target core PCE inflation over the 12 months ending in September. The remaining one-fourth likely reflects persistent effects from the inflationary shocks in recent years. Price pressures had been concentrated in a few categories, but the latest data suggest that these pressures may be broadening.

It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations. But today's consumer price index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer. Tariff effects should further wane going forward. Energy-related price pressures should unwind when the Middle East conflict resolves. And inflation pressures related to the AI buildout seem to persist despite some early signs of slowing. I mostly view these pressures as reflecting relative price shocks in specific sectors of the economy. For example, the AI buildout has quickly shifted investment demand toward specific types of high-tech capital, putting upward pressure on prices due to relatively inelastic supply in the near term. As these shocks wane or unwind and with no inflationary pressures emerging in the labor market, my forecast is for core PCE inflation to move closer to 2 percent next year.

Financial Conditions
Financial conditions have tightened a bit recently because of lower equity prices, higher private interest rates, and a stronger dollar. That tightening comes against a backdrop of increased market volatility. Corporate bond and mortgage rate spreads have widened, and equity valuations in the tech sector have dropped, as investors appear to be reassessing expected returns and the risks associated with increased external financing for AI investment projects.

Economic Outlook and Risks
Looking ahead, my expectation is that policies designed to boost the economic potential of the U.S. economy would continue to support productivity, growth, and business confidence. These policies include pragmatic regulations, lower taxes, and more supportive policies toward businesses. I expect the labor market to remain stable and inflation to slow, as special factors currently holding inflation elevated gradually wane or unwind next year. Over time, I also expect increased AI adoption to raise productivity and put some downward pressure on inflation as lower production costs are passed through to consumer prices.

On risks to the outlook, with the labor market improving since last year, I am more attentive to the inflation side of our mandate. Sustained supply-chain pressures from the AI buildout or greater pass-through of higher energy costs could cause inflation pressures to persist. I can also envision a scenario in which the effects of the Middle East conflict and the tech investment boom wane or unwind quickly. In this scenario, I would also expect a timelier return of core PCE inflation toward our target.

I also see a number of risks to the outlook for economic activity, many originating in financial markets. These risks include a large correction in equity valuations, if returns on AI investment fall short of expectations, and a sharp increase in private longer-term interest rates. Lower equity prices could undermine the resilience in consumer spending. And higher interest rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, like housing and small business investment. I will continue to closely monitor developments in credit and equity markets to assess risks to economic growth and financial stability.

Important Issues for Monetary Policy
I see conditions in energy markets and the AI buildout as two important issues for the economy in the months ahead. Developments in these two areas could have material effects on both sides of our mandate and could influence my views on the path for monetary policy.

Energy Markets
The Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets, impairing the flow of oil and other commodities passing through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for about 20 percent of global oil supply before the conflict—roughly equivalent to total U.S. oil consumption. As tensions rose, Brent oil prices moved up to and above $110 per barrel in the second half of October before dropping sharply last week on optimism that an agreement between the U.S. and Iran could be reached following the midterm elections. Although crude oil flows in the Persian Gulf have recovered to near pre-conflict levels in recent weeks, freight rates and insurance premiums have surged because of more complex logistics and ongoing geopolitical risk, raising the cost of delivered oil to many markets around the world.

Prices for gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel also moved up to near or even above their highs in the spring. These higher prices reflected both higher crude oil prices and wider refining margins, as refineries in both the Persian Gulf and Russia have been damaged as a result of ongoing military conflicts in both regions. Prices for refined products have retraced some of the earlier gains more recently as crude oil prices have receded and margins have shown signs of normalizing.

While the outcomes of these conflicts remain uncertain, my approach is to look through temporary energy-driven inflation, when possible, and to remain alert to signs that it is spreading into broader prices or expectations. If geopolitical tensions persist, energy prices may stay elevated in the near term, increasing risks that core inflation may also stay elevated because of increased pass-through to consumer prices of higher production and transportation costs.

Although the U.S. economy is now a net exporter of oil products and less energy intensive, we could still see an impact on economic activity from higher energy prices. The recent deterioration in consumer sentiment measures suggests households may be internalizing a more persistent reduction in their purchasing power. I would be especially concerned about effects on both sides of our mandate if there were further significant disruptions to energy markets. An escalation of geopolitical tensions could have more meaningful effects on real activity because of higher uncertainty and the larger impact of energy prices on lower- and middle-income consumers.

Even with a quick resolution to the Middle East conflict, it may take some time for energy prices to normalize. Futures markets expect oil prices to decline only gradually, as global oil consumption is projected to exceed supply at least through the end of this year. As inventories have been drawn down, the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has reached a bit less than 50 days of crude oil imports, the lowest level since the early 1980s, reflecting both this year's and the larger 2022 SPR releases. A number of new Gulf pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz are under construction or expansion, with the United Arab Emirates' West–East expansion coming online in early 2027 and most others in 2028 and beyond. Domestic oil production could also continue to rise, which would put downward pressure on fuel costs.

AI Buildout
In remarks earlier this year, I discussed the responsible use of AI in the financial system.4 Today I will describe how this technology is shaping the broader economy. Given the transformative promise of this technology, investment in data centers has boomed and has been a major influence on the U.S. economy. With plans for new data centers continuing to surge, I expect the AI shock to play out over some time. However, as these investments are increasingly being financed with external funds, including off-balance-sheet liabilities, I am also focused on potential risks to the economy and financial stability if revenues from AI customers disappoint.

We may still be in the early days when investment rises rapidly while workers and firms determine the best use cases before we see more meaningful effects on productivity. The boom in data center investment is undeniable, with growth in real business fixed investment strengthening further this year to a pace like the 1990s tech boom. High-tech equipment, software, and data center construction have accounted for the large majority of growth in business investment since 2025, with gains broadening to other categories this year.

AI adoption has grown significantly, especially among larger firms, with about 25 percent of businesses and roughly 10 percent of workers reporting using AI every day in their work. However, use varies greatly across industries and occupations, with stronger adoption in information and other business services sectors. I think there is a risk that some workers will be displaced as firms adopt this technology, even as others see their productivity—and wages—rise. Monetary policy cannot address that transition directly, but it should support a dynamic labor market that facilitates the necessary retraining and mobility of workers across jobs.

AI revenues have been rising quickly but are not yet sufficient to pay for the expense of maintaining existing and developing new AI models and data centers. As capital spending has surged, hyperscalers and other companies have increasingly been sourcing funds from credit and equity markets. And as investors see an increased risk in these investments, the cost of financing has been rising notably.

In addition to financing costs, the AI buildout is also putting upward pressure on a number of price categories. Prices of memory chips, semiconductors, computers, and other electronic products have increased sharply this year—in a few categories by double digits—as demand from data centers has outpaced supply. I expect production capacity to catch up to demand gradually over time.

AI-related debt has been rising rapidly, with notable gains in corporate bonds, private credit, and project finance, and is on track to exceed $800 billion this year. Other obligations, in the form of long-term lease and contract commitments and residual value guarantees, have also surged and their potential payments are estimated at more than three times the amount of debt. Given their strong credit ratings, hyperscalers and large tech firms have assumed off-balance-sheet liabilities to allow smaller and riskier companies to use them as collateral in asset-based financing for data center construction and the purchase of accelerated computing equipment. These connections among AI firms have also been accompanied by hyperscalers and chip designers making equity investments in smaller companies that purchase their products, creating the appearance of circular financing.

The largest U.S. bank holding companies have some exposure to AI-related financing, which is scrutinized during annual supervisory stress tests. Life insurance companies, pension funds, private credit, and mutual funds also have exposure. Most of these entities are well capitalized and have stable funding. But the complex nature of the financing structures makes it difficult to properly assess counterparty risk.

Risks seem to be concentrated in only a few large firms that provide AI services, including AI labs and the hyperscalers. If AI-related revenues fall short of sharply rising costs, especially as public sentiment and local opposition could lead to increased regulation and delays, we could see a sharp correction in equity prices for AI firms, higher financing costs, and reduced access to credit. This shock would likely slow the AI buildout and soften both economic activity and inflation.

We may have already seen some reassessment of expected returns play out in recent weeks as equity valuations dropped, corporate bond spreads widened, and credit default swaps increased for some companies involved in the AI buildout. I will be looking at how momentum in adoption of and investment in this technology evolves and for possible effects on both inflation and employment.

The Path Forward for Monetary Policy
As we think about the path ahead, it is important to remember that over the past two years the U.S. economy has experienced successive inflationary shocks that have not been driven by labor market conditions. Monetary policy cannot offset the direct effects of tariffs and energy costs on inflation, but it plays a central role in containing the second-round effects. Monetary policy also has limited influence on AI-related price pressures. However, in certain segments of AI-intensive sectors, particularly among newer and medium-sized firms, higher interest rates appear to be holding back investment and purchasing decisions.

As I noted earlier, financial conditions have tightened. Against this backdrop, the benefit of additional policy tightening has to be carefully weighed against its costs for interest-rate-sensitive sectors. The October Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices (SLOOS) suggests that the concentration of demand weakness in real estate loan categories reflects existing headwinds in those sectors.5

Time will help us learn more about the durability of momentum in AI-related demand and the evolution of geopolitical risks, both of which could be critical in the months ahead for setting our policy stance. Greater clarity on AI-related financing conditions and the sustainability of AI investments should increase my confidence in future policy decisions. Geopolitical conditions affect commodity markets and the degree of economic uncertainty perceived by households and businesses.

Before our next meeting in December, we will receive the PCE inflation report for October and the employment report for November. Today, I am seeing signs that inflation pressures are persisting, while labor market conditions appear to be firming. This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2 percent. Given the recent market volatility, I will also continue to closely monitor how developments in financial conditions influence the economic outlook.

In the meantime, I will continue to meet with a broad range of contacts to inform my assessment of economic conditions and the appropriate stance of policy. It is important to remember that monetary policy is not on a preset course. At each FOMC meeting, my colleagues and I will evaluate incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the implications for the risks to our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and price stability.

Thank you again for the invitation to join you this afternoon. I look forward to our discussion.

1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) or the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. 

2. See Atlantic Council (2026), "Federal Reserve Vice Chair Michelle Bowman on Modernizing Financial Regulation," AC Front Page event, Washington, October 1. 

3. Note that currently reported GDP growth in the first half of this year may be overestimated by about 0.3 percentage point, reflecting downward revisions in the retail sales annual update that were not folded into the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) 2026 annual revision of the national accounts. 

4. See Michelle W. Bowman (2026), "Artificial Intelligence in the Financial System," (PDF) remarks delivered at the Financial Stability Oversight Council Artificial Intelligence Series Roundtable on Cybersecurity and Risk Management, Washington, May 1. 

5. The October 2026 SLOOS is available on the Board's website at https://www.federalreserve.gov/data/sloos/sloos-202610.htm.

item.title: SEC Announces Enforcement Annual Results For Fiscal Year 2026 - Division Continues To Prioritize Impactful Enforcement Actions And Emphasize Individual Accountability To Deter Misconduct And Strengthen Investor Protection And Market Integrity
item.content:encoded:
The Securities and Exchange Commission today provided its enforcement results for the past fiscal year which ended September 30. Throughout the fiscal year, the SEC’s Division of Enforcement remained focused on its fundamental responsibility: protecting investors, holding wrongdoers accountable, and safeguarding the integrity of the U.S. capital markets. The Division is also continuing to modernize its organization, processes, and technology, and launched several new initiatives in 2026 that will ensure the Division’s effectiveness in the years to come.

Impactful Enforcement

Enforcement actions filed in fiscal year 2026 demonstrate the Division’s continued commitment to rigorous, effective enforcement that focuses on serious and consequential violations of the federal securities laws—including fraud, market manipulation, insider trading, failures and misconduct by gatekeepers, and violations that compromise the integrity of disclosures and financial reporting. The cases emphasize the nature and severity of misconduct, magnitude of investor harm, and pursuit of meaningful remedies. Two-thirds of all standalone enforcement actions filed in fiscal year 2026 included charges against at least one individual, reflecting the Division’s continued commitment to maximizing deterrence and holding wrongdoers accountable. 

In fiscal year 2026, the Commission filed 348 enforcement actions, including 235 standalone actions and 113 “follow-on” administrative proceedings that sought to bar or suspend individuals from participating in certain securities markets activities based on criminal convictions, civil injunctions, or other qualifying orders. The Commission also instituted 13 trading suspensions in response to suspected manipulation involving the securities of Asia-based issuers.

In addition, the Commission obtained orders for monetary relief totaling $1.095 billion, comprised of $752 million in disgorgement and prejudgment interest and $343 million in civil penalties, with $235 million of the disgorgement ordered deemed satisfied by a court in a separate non-SEC action. The SEC also returned approximately $731 million to more than 250,000 harmed investors.

“The success of the SEC’s enforcement program is ultimately measured by how effectively it advances the SEC’s mission, protects investors, holds wrongdoers accountable, and strengthens confidence in our markets,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins. “Enforcement actions and financial remedies are important measures of activity, but they are not the only or most telling measures. Our responsibility is to apply the law fairly and consistently and ensure that our enforcement efforts advance the Commission’s mission. I commend the staff for their dedication to an effective, disciplined enforcement program that serves the investing public.”

“Our focus is on conducting rigorous investigations, pursuing consequential misconduct, and achieving meaningful outcomes for investors,” said David Woodcock, Director of the SEC’s Division of Enforcement. “During the fiscal year, we reviewed our investigative docket, strengthened our investigative capabilities, and launched several new initiatives that will position the Division even more strongly for the future. These efforts have resulted in an enforcement program that is more focused, effective, and prepared to address both longstanding and emerging threats to our markets.”

Positioning the Division of Enforcement for the Future

In fiscal year 2026, the Division worked to modernize its organization and processes to increase its investigative and litigation capacity, address evolving market risks, and deliver more timely, impactful outcomes to ensure the Division’s effectiveness in the years to come. The Division also invested in its leadership ranks with a new leadership training program for supervisors. And with targeted hiring across key skill areas, the Division hired attorneys, accountants, technologists, and data specialists to deepen the Division’s bench expertise and accelerate its critical investigative work.

Organizational Enhancements

In fiscal year 2026, the Division made significant organizational enhancements.

The Division formed the Retail Fraud Working Group (RFWG) to strengthen its ability to identify and address fraudulent schemes—including Ponzi schemes and offering frauds, impersonation scams, broker-dealer misconduct, false and fraudulent filings, and market manipulation schemes—and other misconduct that pose significant risks to everyday investors. Drawing on the expertise of attorneys across the Division, the RFWG employs targeted, data-driven strategies, including Super Intelligence (SI) and the analysis of information from multiple regulatory and law enforcement sources, to uncover potential violations and generate investigative leads for referral throughout the Division. In fiscal year 2026, the RFWG reviewed numerous tips and complaints, generated referrals involving suspected fraud and other violations affecting retail investors, and undertook extensive outreach involving other regulators, industry participants, and investors. Already, more than a dozen new investigations have resulted from the RFWG’s efforts.

In addition, the Division expanded its capacity to address complex accounting and financial reporting fraud schemes as well as other misconduct involving accountants and auditors with a new Financial Reporting and Accounting Unit (FRAU). FRAU combines the skills of attorneys and accountants with deep expertise in accounting standards, issuer disclosures, internal accounting controls, books and records requirements, and auditor responsibilities. This concentration of expertise strengthens the Division’s ability to detect patterns of financial misconduct, promotes a disciplined and consistent approach to evaluating potential violations, and ensures technically rigorous enforcement recommendations. Already, FRAU is improving the Division’s effectiveness by identifying problems earlier in the reporting cycle, building stronger and more analytically precise cases, and accelerating the timeline for delivering meaningful protections for investors. These early returns underscore FRAU’s role as a cornerstone of the Division’s efforts to modernize the enforcement program and an enhanced safeguard for the integrity of the financial reporting ecosystem.

Complementing these enhancements, the Division launched the Office of Super Intelligence and Analytics, a dedicated office designed to bring advanced analytical capability directly into investigative workflows, “force-multiply” resources, and strengthen the Division’s overall capacity to protect investors. The office uses data‑driven techniques and SI tools to identify patterns of misconduct earlier, improve investigative efficiency, and detect emerging threats across markets. Its work includes SI‑enabled anomaly detection, accelerated document and transcript review, and improved blockchain and financial‑flow analysis. The office better positions the Division to address rapidly evolving threats, especially in fraud, cyber, and SI-enabled manipulation schemes

The Division also reorganized its Trial Unit to enhance consistency across the Division’s litigation docket and expand the Division’s overall litigation capacity. Following the reorganization, the Chief Litigation Counsel supervises newly created Deputy Chief Litigation Counsels, who oversee the Division’s litigation attorneys across all the Commission’s offices. The Division also improved the Trial Unit’s case management processes to improve its ability to oversee cases filed across the country.   

Investing in Division Leadership

During fiscal year 2026, the Division invested in its leadership ranks by launching a formal leadership training program for new and experienced supervisors. This program, which will continue beyond the fiscal year, is helping the Division build a deep and capable bench of leaders and preparing its next generation of leadership for success in the years to come.

The Division also instituted a new performance-management process in which Senior Officers participate in bi‑monthly meetings with senior leadership to discuss investigation timelines, milestones, and staffing levels. This process ensures that the Division identifies risks early and completes investigative milestones in a timely and efficient manner, thus achieving meaningful investor protection.

Strengthening Interagency Coordination

The Commission strengthened its reach over the past year through memoranda of understanding (MOU) with key partners. The Commission entered into an MOU with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission that deepens collaboration on enforcement matters involving market integrity and complex financial products, enabling more efficient information‑sharing and joint oversight of misconduct spanning across the securities and derivatives markets. Additionally, the Commission entered into an MOU with the Food and Drug Administration that enhances coordination in monitoring disclosures and compliance issues affecting life‑sciences companies, and reinforces safeguards where securities law intersects with product‑regulatory obligations. The Division also continued its historic close coordination with the PCAOB, ensuring auditor misconduct and audit failures are identified and addressed swiftly and efficiently.

The Division filed numerous enforcement actions in parallel with criminal authorities in fiscal year 2026, seeking complementary relief such as targeted injunctions, asset freezes, and associational bars. The Division also worked closely with overseas regulators and law enforcement in multi‑jurisdictional fraud matters, reflecting the global nature of emerging schemes.

Updated Enforcement Manual

The Division made significant updates to the Enforcement Manual for the first time since 2017. Notably, the updates standardize the Wells process, adding transparency, consistency, and clarity to this important part of the enforcement program; allow simultaneous Commission consideration of settlement recommendations and related waiver requests; and explain the Division’s framework for evaluating cooperation, including the impact of cooperation on civil penalties. As announced, the Division will review the Manual on an annual basis going forward to keep its processes current, fair, and effective.

Rescission of Rule 202.5(e)

The Commission rescinded Rule 202.5(e) of its informal rules of procedures, which provided that the Commission would not settle an enforcement action in which a sanction is imposed unless the defendant or respondent also agreed not to publicly deny the allegations in the complaint or administrative order. Among other things, rescinding Rule 202.5(e) aligned the Commission with the overwhelming majority of federal agencies that do not have a similar rule and provided the SEC more flexibility in settling enforcement actions, which conserves resources, provides certainty, and potentially expedites the return of money to injured investors.

Noteworthy Enforcement Actions

Vigorous Pursuit of Cross-Border Fraud

The Division took decisive action to disrupt foreign bad actors targeting U.S. markets and investors. This work built off the momentum of the Commission launching, in September 2025, the Cross‑Border Task Force, a dedicated enforcement group that protects U.S. investors from transnational bad actors. 

In a host of enforcement actions brought in November 2025 and August 2026, the Commission charged a total of 42 entities in the District of Colorado, two entities in the Southern District of New York, and an entity in the Northern District of New York, for allegedly filing false Forms ADV to feign legitimacy as U.S. advisers and lure retail investors. Several of these entities appeared to be located overseas, as alleged. 

The SEC brought charges against three purported crypto asset trading platforms and four investment clubs for allegedly defrauding retail investors of at least $14 million and funneling those funds overseas in an investment confidence scam that involved soliciting investors through social media using investment tips supposedly generated by SI. The SEC also charged multiple entities, likely operated by individuals overseas, for allegedly defrauding hundreds of retail investors through investment confidence scams on online platforms. The Commission instituted cease-and-desist proceedings against a foreign-based issuer that, according to the order, engaged in sham transactions concerning certain online advertising and marketing that materially overstated its net revenues. 

The SEC also instituted 13 trading suspensions to protect U.S. investors from harm arising out of suspected manipulation in the securities of Asia-based issuers. The trading suspensions involved potential manipulation designed to artificially inflate the price and trading volume of the securities, mostly using social media.   

Combating Harm to Retail Investors

Throughout the fiscal year, the Division concentrated resources on matters that cause real harm to retail investors, including offering frauds, Ponzi schemes, and emerging technology scams. 

For example, in fiscal year 2026, the Commission charged:

  • Goliath Ventures, Inc. and its founder and CEO for allegedly operating a multi-year Ponzi scheme that raised at least $425 million from over 1,300 investors;
  • A founder and his two New Jersey-based companies for allegedly conducting a Ponzi scheme which raised approximately $16 million from more than 200 inexperienced investors, primarily targeting Christians of Ghanaian heritage in New York and New Jersey;
  • AKL Transport LLC, Southern Truck Leasing LLC, and their founder in an alleged Ponzi scheme that raised at least $127 million from approximately 765 investors nationwide. Approximately $33 million of investor funds were allegedly misappropriated for personal use;
  • The founder and CEO of a bitcoin mining business, for allegedly raising over $95.6 million from approximately 6,400 investors through a fraud scheme, and misappropriating $48.5 million of investor funds;
  • Three individuals for their roles in an alleged affinity fraud that raised approximately $47 million from more than 87 investors, primarily members of Orthodox Jewish communities in New Jersey and New York.

Over the past year, the Division intensified its investor-protection efforts in the pre‑IPO secondary market. As investors obtain greater access to private markets, the risk of harm posed by fraudsters and other bad actors in those markets grows as well. In line with this focus, the Commission charged: private fund adviser, Adit Ventures Management, its CEO, and affiliated general partners for allegedly defrauding investors and client funds in connection with investments in pre-IPO shares, including by misappropriating advisory client assets and charging millions in undisclosed fees; private fund adviser, Meyer Global Management, and its CEO for allegedly defrauding investors and client funds in connection with investments in SpaceX and other pre-IPO securities; and boiler room operator, Andrew Spaventa, and three of his entities in an alleged fraud scheme that purportedly offered retail investors an opportunity to invest in shares of pre-IPO private companies while charging hidden fees. In a settled order, the Commission found that a California resident allegedly defrauded investors in a private fund that invested in pre-IPO shares of Palantir Technologies, Inc.

Reinforcing Critical Investor Protection Guardrails

The Commission also brought enforcement actions to reinforce critical investor-protection guardrails, which strengthen compliance by holding market participants accountable for failing to meet their obligations, increase the likelihood that fraud and other misconduct is detected early, and provide meaningful deterrence to would-be bad actors from violating the law. These actions involved the Custody Rule, Regulation Best Interest, privacy and identity‑protection breaches, Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) and Bank Secrecy Act obligations, and blue sheet compliance. These guardrails strengthen deterrence, enable early detection of misconduct, and support effective market oversight. 

Among other enforcement actions, the Commission instituted settled orders against:

  • Registered investment advisers Northeast Financial Group, Inc., and, in a separate action, FamilyWealth Advisers, LLC and FamilyWealth Asset Management, LLC, finding that each violated Section 206(4) of the Advisers Act and Rule 206(4)-2 thereunder (the Custody Rule);

  • Hext Capital Partners, LLC, a registered broker-dealer, finding that it violated Section 15(c)(3) of the Exchange Act and Rule 15c3-1 thereunder (the Net Capital Rule), and its principal owner and managing member, finding that he caused Hext Capital’s violations;

  • Simplify Asset Management, Inc., a registered investment adviser to ETFs, finding that it caused a trust, which had an ownership stake in Simplify, to engage in prohibited affiliate transactions with an ETF client and caused another ETF client to exceed leverage thresholds permitted by Investment Company Act Rule 18f-4.

  • David Lerner Associates, Inc., a registered broker-dealer, finding that it violated Regulation Best Interest in connection with at least 253 recommendations to retail customers to sell Class A mutual fund shares held for less than one year and nearly simultaneously buy Class A mutual fund shares in a different fund family, which imposed new upfront sales charges paid to the firm and its registered representatives;

  • MCB Acquisitions Manager LLC, finding that it failed to timely file a Schedule 13D after it acquired more than five percent of the common stock of a REIT that it planned to take private, and ACM-CPC LLC, finding that it filed an inaccurate Schedule 13D and an untimely amendment to its Schedule 13D in connection with its plan to change control of a company in which it invested; 

  • M Holdings Securities, Inc., a dually registered broker-dealer and investment adviser, finding that it failed to adopt or maintain reasonably designed policies and procedures concerning cybersecurity, the protection of customer information, and identity theft prevention in violation of Rule 30(a) of Regulation S-P (the Safeguards Rule) and Rule 201 of Regulation S-ID (the Identity Theft Red Flags Rule);

  • The New York Stock Exchange LLC, finding that it violated Rule 1001(a)(2)(vii) of Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity (Regulation SCI) and Exchange Act Section 19(g)(1) in connection with an event in which NYSE failed to conduct opening auctions for more than 2,800 securities;

  • Foot Locker, Inc., finding that it violated Rule 21F-17(a) of the Exchange Act, which prohibits any person from taking any action to impede an individual from communicating directly with the Commission staff about a possible securities law violation, by using separation agreements that purported to waive employees’ rights to receive whistleblower awards from the Commission;

  • Registered broker-dealers Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith Incorporated and Canaccord Genuity LLC, finding that they failed to file Suspicious Activity Reports in violation of Section 17(a) of the Exchange Act and Rule 17a-8 thereunder; and

  • Registered broker-dealer Wedbush Securities Inc., finding that it failed to provide complete and accurate securities trading information, known as blue sheet data, to the SEC, in violation of Section 17(a)(1) of the Exchange Act and Rules 17a-4(j) and 17a-25 thereunder.

Strengthening Market Integrity

The Division continued to pursue market manipulation and insider trading, conduct that undermines the fairness and efficiency of markets. Enforcement actions in fiscal year 2026 addressed spoofing, deceptive trading, and misuse of material nonpublic information by employees, gatekeepers, and professionals across industries. Consistent with its return to basics, the Division prioritized these matters so that investors can expect accountability for abusive practices.

In fiscal year 2026, the Commission charged:

  • 21 individuals for their alleged involvement in a decade-long insider trading scheme involving information misappropriated from multiple global law firms and resulting in millions of dollars in illicit profits;
  • In separate actions, a California day trader, a Las Vegas man, a resident of Tujunga, California, and a day trader operating from San Juan, Puerto Rico, for allegedly orchestrating fraudulent “spoofing” schemes to manipulate stock prices and generate ill-gotten gains;
  • Three Pakistani and U.S. nationals for allegedly carrying out two market manipulation schemes and, with three associates, an approximately $41 million insider trading scheme involving nine potential corporate acquisitions;
  • The former Chief Revenue Officer of Doximity, Inc., a digital platform provider for U.S. medical professionals, for allegedly trading Doximity stock ahead of a quarterly earnings call based on material nonpublic information concerning Doximity’s lower-than-expected sales;
  • A nuclear engineer formerly employed by Constellation Energy Corporation, for allegedly trading in Constellation’s securities based on material nonpublic information relating to Constellation’s confidential project to potentially restart its nuclear power plant at Three Mile Island; and
  • A biopharmaceutical company employee that allegedly traded in advance of an acquisition announcement based on material nonpublic information he learned while serving on a due diligence team for a potential transaction.

The Commission also instituted settled orders against:

  • An attorney finding that he traded in the securities of his client based upon material nonpublic information regarding a pending acquisition that he learned in connection with representing the company in an unrelated legal matter;
  • An employee in ImmunityBio Inc.’s Research and Development Department and a documentary filmmaker employed by ImmunityBio, finding that each illegally traded in advance of an announcement that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration had decided to delay approval of ImmunityBio’s drug candidate; and
  • An employee of Jazz Pharmaceuticals plc, finding that he traded in Jazz securities in advance of an acquisition announcement based on material nonpublic information he learned while serving on the due diligence team.

Promoting Accurate Disclosure, Accounting, and Financial Reporting

In fiscal year 2026, the Commission filed settled charges against Archer-Daniels-Midland Company and two former executives, and a litigated action charging a third former executive, for materially inflating the performance of a key business segment that the company touted to investors as an important growth driver. The Commission also instituted a settled order against two former public company executives finding that they failed to disclose to the company’s auditor at least $290,000 in personal and/or unauthorized expenses paid by the company.

The Commission also charged:

  • Financial technology company, RYVYL, Inc., and its two founders for allegedly making fraudulent disclosures in RYVYL’s public filings;

  • Two former executives of now-defunct Near Intelligence, Inc. for allegedly inflating revenue in a financial accounting and disclosure fraud scheme, along with Near Intelligence’s largest customer and its former CEO with aiding and abetting the alleged fraud;

  • Electric vehicle manufacturer Battle Motors, Inc., and its CEO for allegedly making materially misleading statements in connection with a convertible debt offering that raised $112.5 million from two outside investors; and

  • Lottery.com, Inc., three former executives, and the CEO of a SPAC for allegedly conducting a fraudulent scheme and making false statements in connection with a SPAC merger.

The Division also reinforced accounting and auditing standards. For example, the Commission instituted a settled action against an audit engagement partner, finding that the partner’s negligent conduct during audits of the now-defunct crypto asset trading platform FTX resulted in a violation of Generally Accepted Accounting Principles; audit firm EisnerAmper LLP, finding that it failed to perform an audit of a mutual fund’s financial statements in accordance with PCAOB auditing standards; and a New Jersey-based CPA, finding that he failed to comply with the Commission’s and PCAOB’s auditor independence rules as well as several other PCAOB audit standards.

Addressing Misconduct by Investment Advisers and Safeguarding Investors in Private Funds

The Division remained focused on monitoring for and addressing misconduct by investment advisers, including misappropriated client assets, inadequate safeguarding of assets, misleading or inadequate disclosures, undisclosed fees and expenses, fraudulent valuations and mismarking, and undisclosed conflicts of interest. 

Notable enforcement actions in fiscal year 2026 include settled actions instituted against:

  • Three Florida investment advisory firms and their owner, Riadh Fakhoury, finding that they made false claims to investors in venture capital funds they managed that their investments were “low risk, high return,” including by touting co-investments by established institutional investors in the same private technology companies that had not occurred;
  • New York-based investment adviser, Papamarkou Wellner Asset Management, Inc., finding that it failed to comply with the terms of its advisory agreements relating to advisory fee calculations, provided disclosures to clients that were materially inconsistent with the firm’s actual advisory fee offset practices, and failed to implement certain written compliance policies and procedures;
  • A former Illinois-based registered investment adviser to private funds, Madison Capital Funding LLC, finding that it sold loans to private fund clients without reasonably determining whether those trades were at fair market value, contrary to its obligations under its advisory agreements and representations to investors;
  • A former registered investment adviser representative from North Carolina, finding that he failed to adequately disclose conflicts of interest in connection with advising clients on the merits of investing in private real estate securities offerings while receiving nearly $1.5 million in compensation from certain sponsors of the offerings; and
  • Arizona-based investment adviser Foundations Investment Advisors, LLC and its former CEO, Bryon E. Rice, finding that they failed to disclose conflicts of interest—including a profit-sharing interest that Rice held and an expense sharing agreement between Foundations and four ETFs—related to investments that it recommended to advisory clients.

The Commission also charged:

  • Two San Francisco Bay Area private fund manager executives for allegedly orchestrating an offering fraud that raised more than $80 million from approximately 190 mostly retail investors, many of whom were retired senior citizens, and making misrepresentations to investors in two private funds; and
  • A former Oregon investment adviser representative for allegedly misappropriating more than $800,000 in securities from his investment advisory and brokerage clients through a sham investment program he created.

Holding Individual Bad Actors Accountable

Holding individuals accountable remains one of the Commission’s most effective deterrents. Two-thirds of the standalone enforcement actions brought by the Commission this year included claims against at least one individual, including founders and CEOs in major Ponzi and offering fraud cases, senior executives in financialreporting cases, and gatekeepers such as accountants, auditors, and investment adviser personnel whose failures or misconduct contributed to investor harm. Most of the enforcement actions previously discussed in this release involved charges against individuals. 

Additional examples include:

  • Charges against the former CEO, CFO, and Senior Director of Finance of Texas-based Tricolor Holdings, LLC, for their roles in an alleged multi-year scheme to defraud investors by double pledging hundreds of millions of dollars of subprime auto loans to multiple asset-backed securities offerings and lenders;

  • A settled order against the former CEO and CFO of biopharmaceutical company Spero Therapeutics Inc., finding that they made misleading statements and omissions regarding feedback received from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Spero’s lead drug candidate;

  • A settled order against a former CFO of The Bancorp, Inc., finding that he directed the company to file its Form 10-K—which represented that the audit of the company’s financial statements was complete and included audit opinions and consents from the company’s auditors—despite knowing that the auditors had not provided final approval to include their audit opinions and consents; and

  • Charges against three former executives of Ammo, Inc. n/k/a Outdoor Holding Co., for their roles in an alleged accounting and disclosure fraud in which they made repeated materially false and misleading statements in Ammo’s public SEC filings and financial statements that generally had the purpose of hiding or obfuscating unfavorable information about the management and operations of the company.

Encouraging Prompt Remediation and Cooperation

The Commission continued to emphasize that prompt remediation and meaningful cooperation can accelerate investigations and influence charging and penalty decisions. Recent enforcement matters emphasized the factors that the Commission considers when evaluating cooperation, such as prompt self-reporting, swift and thorough remediation, and early, proactive engagement with staff. Several enforcement actions in fiscal year 2026 reflect calibrated penalties and charging decisions that took remediation and cooperation into account.

For example, in a settled order, the Commission found that CBIZ Inc. had made unregistered offers and sales of securities but imposed no civil penalty in acknowledging the cooperation afforded to the Commission staff and remedial acts promptly undertaken by CBIZ. Likewise, the Commission described extensive remedial steps taken and imposed no civil penalties in an order against Ammo, Inc. n/k/a Outdoor Holding Company for misleadingly failing to disclose certain information on Forms 10-K and presenting materially misstated financial statements on Forms 10-K and Forms 8-K; and in an order against Key Tronic Corporation and two of its senior executives, for books and records and internal controls violations related to false entries in the company’s inventory system that improperly increased income. In a settled order against Nipun Kumar Jami, the Commission found that Jami traded in advance of an acquisition based on material nonpublic information obtained from his spouse and imposed a civil penalty equal to half of Jami’s illicit profits, acknowledging his voluntary self-report to the staff approximately one month after the acquisition was announced and cooperation in the Commission’s investigation. 

The Commission also held firms that failed to promptly remediate known deficiencies accountable. For example, the Commission imposed a $20 million civil penalty in a settled order against dually registered UBS Financial Services Inc., finding that UBSFS failed to adequately monitor its customers’ FX wire transactions for possible suspicious transactions, as required by its own anti-money laundering policies and procedures, and—even after engaging a consulting firm to remediate deficiencies in its data for customer FX wire transactions and conduct a “lookback” to determine if it was required to file additional SARs—UBSFS failed to timely file “lookback” SARS concerning thousands of suspicious transactions. 

Likewise, the Commission also imposed a $100 million civil penalty against Western Asset Management Company, LLC, finding that it failed to take reasonable steps to detect and prevent a cherry-picking scheme despite being aware that the trading and allocation practices of its former co-Chief Investment Officer diverged from those of other portfolio managers at the firm.

Office of the Whistleblower

Since its enactment in 2011, the SEC’s whistleblower program has become an integral part of the Division’s crucial work to detect and prosecute wrongdoing and protect investors.  Whistleblowers often provide significant information that either alerts the Commission to possible securities law violations or substantially contributes to an existing investigation.  Indeed, high-quality whistleblower tips have resulted in impactful SEC enforcement actions covering a broad range of misconduct and led to more than $11 billion in financial remedies ordered by the Commission since inception of the program.  Participation in the whistleblower program remains strong: In fiscal year 2026, the Commission received approximately 26,000 whistleblower tips and awarded more than $158 million to 65 individual whistleblowers, the highest number of individual whistleblowers since fiscal year 2023.

Litigation Highlights

The Division prevailed in several cases at trial, on summary judgment, and in the remedies phase in fiscal year 2026, including:

Trials 

SEC v. Robert Brian Watson (D. Colo.) 

In January 2026, after a five-day trial, a jury found defendants R. Brian Watson and Northstar Commercial Partners, a real estate company Watson owned, liable for intentional securities fraud. The Commission charged Watson and Northstar in August 2022 for allegedly misrepresenting their own investments in securities offerings to fund various real estate projects across the country. 

As demonstrated at trial, Watson and Northstar defrauded investors in 11 different offerings over the course of about 36 months. Defendants told investors that Watson “co-invested” in every real estate offering by investing his personal funds in Northstar-sponsored real estate projects alongside investors who were also investing in common equity. The statements were false and misleading because Watson did not co-invest his personal funds and have “skin in the game” as promised to investors.

SEC v. Ismael Zarco Sanchez (S.D. Tex.)

In February 2026, after a four-day trial, a jury found defendant Ismael Sanchez liable for securities fraud and registration violations. The Commission charged Sanchez and 16 other individuals in March 2024 for their alleged roles in a $300 million Ponzi scheme that involved Houston, Texas-based CryptoFX LLC and targeted more than 40,000 predominately Latino investors.

As demonstrated at trial, Sanchez was a lead salesperson for the CryptoFX Ponzi scheme that involved promises to trade investor funds in the crypto asset and foreign exchange markets, but in reality used investor money to make Ponzi payments, pay commissions to salespeople, and fund personal expenses. The office in Chicago that Sanchez led raised tens of millions of dollars from investors.

Summary Judgment

SEC v. Brian Hutchison (D.D.C)

In August 2026, the District Court for the District of Columbia granted the Commission’s motion for summary judgment and found that Brian K. Hutchison violated Section 10(b) of the Exchange Act and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, among other charges. The Commission charged Hutchison, then-CEO of RTI Surgical Holdings, Inc., in August 2022 for allegedly masking RTI’s disappointing sales numbers by shipping future orders ahead of schedule to accelerate, or "pull forward," revenue and then failing to disclose this practice to investors. In June 2020, RTI restated its public financial statements from 2014 through 2019 to correct errors caused by this practice. 

Remedies 

SEC v. Robert Newell (C.D. Cal.)

In May 2026, following the entry of a bifurcated consent judgment enjoining Robert Newell from violating Section 17(a) of the Securities Act; Section 10(b) of the Exchange Act and Rule 10b-5 thereunder; and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of the Advisers Act and Rule 206(4)-8 thereunder, the District Court for the Central District of California granted the Commission’s motion for the entry of a final judgment ordering Newell liable for disgorgement in the amount of $668,300, plus prejudgment interest thereon of $254,067, and a civil penalty of $668,300, and enjoining him for five years from directly or indirectly participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any security, except for purchases or sales for his own personal accounts. The Commission charged Newell, a fund manager, and his prior firm, Black Hawk Funding, Inc., in July 2023 with engaging in undisclosed misuses of investor funds, making Ponzi-like payments, and distributing misleading disclosure documents to investors in connection with three cannabis-related private fund offerings. Newell allegedly misappropriated at least approximately $668,300 of investor money. 

SEC v. Trevon Brown, et al. (S.D.N.Y.)

In July 2026, following the entry of a bifurcated consent judgment enjoining Michael Noble from violating Section 5 of the Securities Act and Section 15(a) of the Exchange Act, the District Court for the Southern District of New York granted the Commission’s motion for monetary relief in its entirety, ordering Noble to pay disgorgement in the amount of $731,281, prejudgment interest in the amount of $293,703.36, and a civil penalty in the amount of $50,000. The Commission charged Noble and other co-defendants in May 2021 for their involvement in the promoting and acting as unregistered brokers for the BitConnect digital asset platform “lending program.” 

SEC v. Aron Govil (S.D.N.Y.)

In January 2026, following the entry of a bifurcated consent judgment against Aron Govil imposing certain injunctive and other relief in 2021, the entry of a final judgment in 2022, and the Second Circuit’s 2023 decision vacating the judgment and remanding the case for a determination of pecuniary harm, the District Court for the Southern District of New York granted the Commission’s renewed motion for imposing remedies in its entirety, including $6,670,977 in disgorgement and $3,037,615.59 in prejudgment interest. The Commission charged Govil, the founder and former CEO of Cemtrex, Inc., in July 2021 with misappropriating over $7 million in investor funds and misrepresenting how offering proceeds would be used. The court found that the SEC’s evidence established pecuniary harm, as was required under the Second Circuit’s standard at that time.

item.title: New York Governor Hochul Declares New York Will Lead the Nation in AI Science and Safety; Launches New Research Institute
item.content:encoded:
• New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research Will Bring Together More than 80 Researchers Across New York to Use Empire AI to Test and Evaluate Advanced AI Systems and Safety Frameworks
  • World-Renowned Computer Scientists Greg Morrisett and Jeannette Wing Will Serve as Interim Co-Directors
  • New Portal Opens for Large Frontier AI Companies to Register and Comply with RAISE Safety, Transparency and Reporting Requirements
  • Builds on Governor Hochul’s Nation-Leading AI Safety Agenda, Including the RAISE Act Which Requires Large Frontier AI Developers to Meet Strict Safety, Transparency and Reporting Standards

Governor Kathy Hochul today launched a first-of-its-kind statewide effort to advance artificial intelligence science and safety – the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research based at State University of New York’s (SUNY) Binghamton University. The Center will bring together unprecedented academic expertise to advance AI safety research, accelerate scientific discovery, and independently test advanced AI systems for safety and security.

“While the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable,” Governor Hochul said. “The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word. That's why we are bringing together our world-class researchers and the computing power of Empire AI to independently test powerful AI systems, understand their risks and put that knowledge to work protecting New Yorkers.”

Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said, “New York is uniquely positioned to answer one of the defining challenges of our time: ensuring the world’s most powerful AI systems are safe, reliable, and grounded in rigorous science. We are harnessing the power of Empire AI and the collaborative strength of our academic institutions to advance AI research and open new paths to scientific discovery. Independent testing will help researchers understand what increasingly powerful systems can do and how to use them safely. ”

Greg Morrisett of Cornell Tech and Jeannette Wing of Columbia University, two internationally recognized leaders in computer science and cybersecurity, will lead the Center as interim co-directors. At the Governor’s direction, they will bring together more than 80 leading scientists from colleges and research institutions across New York State with expertise in AI safety, security and computer science. The Center, based at Binghamton University, will convene researchers to address AI safety issues and ensure New York is pushing forward not only AI innovation, but also security. The Center is supported by the advanced computing power of Empire AI, Governor Hochul’s $500 million public-private initiative to drive AI research for public good.

The New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research (NYCAIRR) will address the fundamental and growing challenge of assessing the safety, security, and operation of increasingly powerful AI systems. That mission will be pursued through independent testing of frontier AI systems, foundational scientific research, and the training of a new generation of AI safety experts. The Center will aim to evaluate both the safety of today's AI systems, and develop the scientific tools, measurements and standards needed to evaluate increasingly powerful systems as the technology evolves. Its work will help advance the responsible use of AI in fields ranging from medicine and scientific discovery to critical infrastructure, while providing public officials with objective evidence to inform policy decisions about AI safety and accountability.

The Center’s founding mission is to advance the science of AI and use AI to accelerate discoveries across scientific fields. The statewide initiative announced today builds on that foundation, supporting the Center’s research to independently evaluate advanced AI systems. Its research will focus on understanding how these increasingly powerful systems work, developing ways to test their safety and security, ensuring they behave as intended, and exploring how AI can be used responsibly to advance scientific discovery. One of the Center’s first objectives is a national recruiting effort for experts who focus on foundational limits and mathematical theory, formal methods and verification, agentic and complex systems, hardware security and privacy, interpretability and alignment, and scientific AI and biosecurity.

Governor Hochul first announced the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research in January with a historic $30 million philanthropic gift from a group of donors led by Binghamton alumnus and Bloomberg LP co-founder Tom Secunda, paired with an initial $25 million research investment from SUNY and operating capital from New York State.

Morrisett, Dean and Vice Provost of Cornell Tech, and Wing, Executive Vice President for Research at Columbia University, have spent their careers studying how complex computing systems operate, where they can fail and how to make them more secure. As interim co-directors, they will guide the Center's scientific agenda, oversee its independent evaluation work, and help build a statewide network of researchers who will continue working at their home institutions.

Additionally, the new Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) launched its online portal for large frontier AI developers to register with New York State by January 1, 2027. Under the RAISE Act, all frontier AI developers operating in New York are subject to safety and transparency requirements, with additional obligations for large frontier developers. Large frontier developers are required to register through the newly released RAISE Portal by January 1, 2027. Beginning in January, large frontier developers will also be required to publish safety frameworks on their websites, and all frontier developers will be required to report critical safety incidents and publish model transparency reports. Additionally, DIGIT published a new website outlining requirements for frontier AI developers operating in the state.

This announcement builds on Governor Hochul’s nation-leading AI safety agenda, which also includes implementation of New York’s RAISE Act. Under that new law, large frontier AI developers will be required to register with the state and comply with strict safety, transparency and reporting requirements — including New York’s strongest-in-the-nation requirement to report any critical safety incident within 72 hours. The Governor also established the first-in-the-nation DIGIT Office to implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI Developers.

New York State Department of Financial Services Acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow said, “The New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research represents another important step in advancing AI safety. DFS is proud to lead the implementation of the RAISE Act through the new DIGIT Office. We look forward to working closely with the Center under Governor Hochul’s leadership.”

At the State’s request, NYCAIRR will be able to provide expertise, assessments and evidence that can assist in informing state policy making and oversight of frontier AI Developers. For example, NYCAIRR will coordinate with DIGIT to begin reviewing AI Developers’ published safety frameworks and providing recommendations on ways to strengthen requirements.

SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. said, “SUNY is at the cutting edge of advancing AI for the public good. Through Governor Hochul’s steadfast leadership and the Center for AI Responsibility and Research at the State University of New York at Binghamton, SUNY will help ensure New York State is a national and global leader in advancing AI safety and security.”

The SUNY Board of Trustees said, “As AI becomes ever more present in New Yorkers’ daily lives, we have a responsibility to ensure this technology is constantly evaluated and harnessed safely. SUNY is leading the way on research excellence, and through the strong support of Governor Hochul and with institutions like the Center for AI Responsibility and Research at the State University of New York at Binghamton, we will be better equipped to ensure that as AI advances, it will do so in safe and transparent ways that benefit New Yorkers.”

State University of New York at Binghamton President Anne D’Alleva said, “The Center for AI Responsibility and Research at the State University of New York at Binghamton will help New York State lead the nation in AI transparency and security. Thanks to the leadership of Governor Hochul and with gratitude to our alumnus Tom Secunda, Binghamton University is proud to host this transformative center and welcome the world-class researchers who will help us continue to serve as global leaders in advancing the public good.”

item.title: Ontario Securities Commission Publishes The First Article In Its Q-Bits Series Alongside A Technical Report On Quantum Computing Risks And Opportunities To Help Market Participants Prepare For The Quantum Future
item.content:encoded:
The Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) today published the first article in its OSC Q-Bits series, alongside a technical report examining the risks and opportunities that quantum computing may present for capital market participants. The OSC Q-Bits series will include articles that examine the latest developments in quantum technologies and their implications for capital markets.

The publication of this article by the OSC marks the launch of its new series of articles called OSC Q-Bits. Quantum Computing and Capital Markets: Opportunities, Risks, and Timelines to Readiness provides a plain language summary of the technical report and outlines the oversight role the OSC can play as quantum technologies are developed. It examines the growing threat that malicious actors may collect and store encrypted information today with the expectation that future quantum computers could be capable of decrypting it, called the “harvest now, decrypt later” strategy.

The technical report, Impact of Advancements in Quantum Computing on its Potential Use in Capital Markets, highlights how quantum computing is advancing and what those developments could mean for Ontario's capital markets. While quantum computing has not yet delivered a production-capable economic advantage for financial markets, rapid progress in technology suggests firms should start assessing both the opportunities and risks associated with the technology.

"Effective regulation requires looking around corners and helping market participants understand emerging risks before they become immediate challenges," said Grant Vingoe, Chief Executive Officer of the OSC. "Quantum computing has the potential to drive significant innovation across the economy, including financial services. At the same time, firms need to be thinking today about how future advances could affect cybersecurity, data protection and operational resilience. Early preparation will help support confidence in Ontario's capital markets as these technologies continue to develop."

The report was prepared with the OSC’s regulatory and capital markets perspective combined with the specialized technical expertise of softwareQ Inc. evolutionQ Inc., and the Institute for Quantum Computing at the University of Waterloo.

The OSC Q-Bits series is designed to help investors, registrants, and market participants better understand developments in quantum technologies and their potential implications for Ontario's capital markets.

The report and Q-Bits article are available on the OSC website.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is quantum computing?

Quantum computing is a form of computing that uses the principles of quantum mechanics to process information, enabling certain types of calculations that may be infeasible or impractical for classical computers.

What is "harvest now, decrypt later"?

"Harvest now, decrypt later" refers to a strategy where cybercriminals collect encrypted data today and store it for future decryption. The concern is that advances in quantum computing could eventually allow certain forms of encryption to be broken, potentially exposing sensitive information that remains valuable over long periods.

Why should firms be preparing now if large-scale quantum computers do not yet exist?

Transitioning critical systems, infrastructure and cryptographic tools can take years. Organizations that begin planning early will be better positioned to manage future technology changes, protect sensitive information and maintain operational resilience as quantum computing capabilities evolve.

What steps can registrants and financial businesses take today?

Firms can begin by understanding where and how encryption is used across their operations, identifying sensitive long-term data, monitoring developments in post-quantum cryptography, and incorporating quantum-related risks into existing cybersecurity and risk management programs.

The mandate of the OSC is to provide protection to investors from unfair, improper or fraudulent practices, to foster fair, efficient and competitive capital markets and confidence in the capital markets, to foster capital formation, and to contribute to the stability of the financial system and the reduction of systemic risk. Investors are urged to check the registration of any persons or company offering an investment opportunity and to review the OSC investor materials available at www.osc.ca.

item.title: Appointments To BIS Global Payments Standard-Setting Body And Consultative Council For The Americas
item.content:encoded:
• Bank of Korea Governor Hyun Song Shin appointed Chair of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) for a three-year term from 1 November.
  • Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem’s role as Chair of the Consultative Council for the Americas (CCA) of the BIS extended until 31 March 2027. Santiago Bausili, Governor of the Central Bank of Argentina, appointed CCA Chair from 1 April 2027, for two years.

The central bank Governors of the Global Economy Meeting (GEM) at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) have appointed Bank of Korea Governor Hyun Song Shin as Chair of the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) for a renewable three-year term.

The CPMI brings together central banks from around the world to monitor and analyse developments in payment, clearing and settlement systems and to develop international standards and guidance. 

Mr Shin took up his new role on 1 November 2026. He succeeds Fabio Panetta, Governor of the Bank of Italy and Chair of the BIS Board of Directors. 

In addition, the Board of Directors has extended the term of Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada, as Chair of the Consultative Council for the Americas (CCA) until 31 March 2027.

The Board has also appointed Santiago Bausili, Governor of the Central Bank of Argentina, as CCA Chair starting 1 April 2027, for a two-year term. 

The CCA was established in May 2008 as an advisory committee to the BIS Board of Directors. It comprises the Governors of the eight BIS member central banks in the Americas: Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru and the United States. 

The BIS Representative Office for the Americas, located in Mexico City, provides the secretariat for the CCA.
