item.title: UK Financial Conduct Authority: Man Sentenced Over £154m Fake Takeover Bid Targeting UK-Listed Company
item.content:encoded:
Christopher Woolcott has today been given a 2-year prison sentence, suspended for 2 years, after staging a £154m fake takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration Inc.

He was also ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and to pay costs of £4,627.73.

Mr Woolcott built a sizeable stake in Touchstone, an oil and gas listed company. He then launched a bogus bid to drive up its share price. To give the bid credibility, Mr Woolcott invented several identities, forged takeover documents using Chat GPT and met Touchstone’s chief executive at a central London hotel under a false name. Touchstone ultimately determined that the bid was not legitimate.

Had his plan succeeded, he stood to gain as much as £70,000 through the sale of his shares.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) used a combination of its transaction reporting data, phone records, receipts, CCTV footage and evidence seized to identify Mr Woolcott as the person behind the fraud.

Investigators traced three phone numbers used by different supposed individuals to contact Touchstone, to the same handset, and combined voter-register, open source research and FCA trading data to narrow down potential suspects. A parking payment also placed Mr Woolcott’s car near a Ryman store where the forged documents were sent from.

Searches of Mr Woolcott's home and workplace later recovered the mobile phone linked to the fabricated identities, including a purported private equity partner, his supposed colleague and a fictitious solicitor.

Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Mr Woolcott's fake takeover bid was a calculated attempt to profit by manipulating the market.

'Our investigators followed an extensive evidence trail, exposed the fraud and identified the person behind the ruse.

‘Anyone tempted to manipulate our markets should know that we are fully committed to identifying, investigating and taking action against those who seek to break the law.'

In sentencing, Judge Karu said Mr Woolcott’s operation was deliberate, sophisticated, and planned in which four false identities and forged documents were used to hoodwink Touchstone Exploration Inc with a false takeover bid.

Mr Woolcott pleaded guilty on 10 September 2026 to 1 count of fraud by false representation and 3 counts of making a false instrument.

The investigation demonstrates how the FCA uses its full range of enforcement powers to disrupt financial crime and protect market integrity.

The FCA opened its criminal investigation in March 2025, formally charged Mr Woolcott 16 months later and secured guilty pleas within 18 months of launching the case.

Background

  1. Christopher Woolcott, of Greenwich, London, was born on 23 April 1982.
  2. On 10 September 2026, Woolcott pleaded guilty at Westminster Magistrates’ Court to:
    • 1 count of fraud by false representation, contrary to sections 1 and 2 of the Fraud Act 2006; and
    • 3 counts of making a false instrument, contrary to sections 1 and 6 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981.  
  3. Fraud by false representation is punishable by a fine and/or up to 10 years’ imprisonment.
  4. Making a false instrument is punishable on indictment by a fine and/or up to 10 years’ imprisonment.
  5. On 10 November 2026 at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Woolcott was sentenced to:
    • a 2 year sentence, suspended for 2 years, and ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and pay costs of £4627.73; and 
    • a 14 months custodial sentence for each of the three forgery offences, to run concurrently with the two year suspended sentence. 
  6. The FCA opened its criminal investigation in March 2025.
  7. Touchstone Exploration Inc is listed on AIM and the Toronto Stock Exchange. It was not under investigation by the FCA in connection with this case.
  8. Read the previous FCA press release: Man pleads guilty to fraud and forgery offences relating to fake takeover approach.
  9. Tackling market abuse and financial crime is a priority under the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

item.title: Solidus Labs Named Market Surveillance Provider For Formation Securities' Tokenized Securities Venue On Solana - Formation’s Public Notice Under The SEC Innovation Exemption Names Solidus To Monitor Tokenized NMS Stock Trading Across AMM Liquidity Pools
item.content:encoded:
Solidus Labs is pleased to share that it has been selected as the market surveillance provider for Formation Securities LLC’s Tokenized Securities Venue (TSV) on Solana under the SEC’s Innovation Exemption.

Formation published its Public Notice of Tokenized Securities Venue on November 9, 2026, naming Solidus as its market surveillance provider. Under the Notice, Formation “will implement reasonable measures to monitor trading activity and flag potential price and volume manipulation, insider trading, or other abusive trading activity in Tokenized NMS Stock, utilizing Solidus’ Trade Surveillance platform.” Formation will also use Solidus’ platform to investigate any flagged activity.

The venue will support secondary trading of tokenized NMS stocks through permissioned automated market maker (AMM) liquidity pools. Trading will run 24/7 and is expected to begin in early 2027. Tokenized shares of Exodus Movement (EXOD), Forward Industries (FWDI) and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) are expected at launch.

“We’re proud to support Formation in ensuring that tokenized securities trading maintains the same levels of investor protections and market integrity as any securities market,” said Asaf Meir, Founder and CEO of Solidus Labs, “New market structures always come with new challenges to market integrity, requiring modern, fit-for-purpose trade surveillance practices that can operate across onchain and offchain, 24/7 and highly fragmented environments. Solidus is delighted to provide the right tools for this challenge.”

An AMM has no order book. Tokenized securities’ novel market structure introduces new trade monitoring nuances, which legacy surveillance technology, heavily focused on order-book monitoring, are not effective in addressing. Working with Formation, Solidus HALO will read liquidity pools directly from the chain, covering swaps, liquidity changes, and the wallets behind them. Solana brings speed and 24/7 settlement to equities, and HALO brings the oversight to match.

For TSVs, surveillance is a business enabler. Independent surveillance like Solidus HALO signals trust to issuers before they decide whether to object. It backs the surveillance disclosure in the TSV Notice, and it gives liquidity providers a reason to commit capital.

item.title: AI Bubble Fears Rattle Markets, But Bitcoin Analysts See A Longer-Term Upside
item.content:encoded:
Concerns about an AI bubble intensified last week, sending markets into risk-off mode and dragging crypto lower, according to Marc des Ligneris, Managing Director at Coinshares.

Two developments appeared to drive the shift in sentiment. Democratic efforts to regulate the sector were read as a likely brake on the pace of AI development, at a time when Chinese models are keeping up. At the same time, investors grew wary of the circular nature of many AI deals, in which the same players fund, supply and buy from each other.

Options market signals lingering caution

Des Ligneris pointed to data on Bitcoin options as evidence of the nervousness. The measure he highlighted is the number of days with a positive 25-delta, one-month skew, which shows how much more investors pay for downside protection (puts) than for upside exposure (calls).

Skew fell back to neutral over the summer after the August squeeze. In the last cycle, he noted, that kind of normalisation marked the start of the bull market. This time, however, the pattern has not held so far. Skew has risen again, suggesting investors are still paying up to hedge. Sentiment data, which fell sharply last week, tell a similar story.

Short-term pressure, long-term tailwind?

"In the short term, if the AI correction deepens, Bitcoin's risk-on profile could weigh on it," des Ligneris said.

He argued that the second-round effects matter more. Slower AI spending would quickly expose an economy that is already fragile outside the AI sector. A sharp downturn usually ends in a large injection of liquidity, which has historically been one of the strongest tailwinds for Bitcoin.

item.title: BNP Paribas’ Securities Services Business Advances Digital Tax Reporting With RAQUEST Ahead Of MiKaDiv
item.content:encoded:
BNP Paribas’ Securities Services business is further digitalizing and industrializing its tax reporting capabilities ahead of the implementation of Germany’s new MiKaDiv reporting procedure on 1 January 2027, extending its existing collaboration with RAQUEST.

The implementation of RAQUEST’s MiKaDiv solution will support Securities Services – a leading global custodian and one of Germany’s largest custodians – across its different reporting roles, as part of its broader approach to delivering efficient, secure and scalable tax services for clients.

BNP Paribas already leverages RAQUEST’s STTI Gateway, a modular interface for the digital transmission of reclaim applications to European tax authorities that have digitalized their refund processes. The MiKaDiv implementation extends this collaboration to withholding tax reporting. 

One solution for every role in the custody chain 

BNP Paribas’ Securities Services business operates in several roles at once, and each carries its own MiKaDiv reporting requirements. As a German sub-custodian, BNP Paribas will report directly to the German Federal Central Tax Office (BZSt) on behalf of its clients. 

As a sub-custodian in other European countries and a global custodian, BNP Paribas’ Securities Services business offers custody services to its clients holding their assets with various (I)CSDs and sub-custodians. To this end, MiKaDiv reports and responses are exchanged with multiple (I)CSDs and custodians. 

In addition, BNP Paribas’ Securities Services business will provide indirect MiKaDiv reporting to its intermediary clients benefitting from tax reclaim and relief at source. In this role, reporting requests from intermediaries in the payment chain are validated, processed, and incorporated into the upstream reporting.

RAQUEST’s MiKaDiv suite supports BNP Paribas’ Securities Services business to meet its own high standards for regulatory compliance, accurate tax reporting and first-class client service even more effectively.  

“With MiKaDiv, reporting obligations along the custody chain are changing fundamentally. Institutions with several roles need technology that can handle this complexity in an integrated way. BNP Paribas’ Securities Services business brings all its MiKaDiv reporting needs together in one suite across the business line. With the STTI Gateway already in place, we can build on a proven foundation,” says Alexander Lerch, Co-Founder and CEO of RAQUEST. 

“We strongly believe in the digitalisation of tax processes, including our interactions with tax authorities, to automate the exchange of tax information and make it more secure. By integrating RAQUEST’s MiKaDiv suite, we further digitalise and industrialise our tax reporting, as a first step towards the implementation of the EU FASTER Directive in 2030,” says Mariangela Fumagalli, Head of Asset Servicing Product and Custody Regulatory Solutions, Securities Services, BNP Paribas.

Built on a resilient, cloud-native platform, DTCC’s EU-MiFID ARM is designed to help firms simplify complex reporting workflows, improve data quality and achieve greater confidence in their regulatory reporting. Hillery added, “With DTCC’s MiFID ARM solutions, firms can streamline their approach to regulatory obligations, backed by resilient technology, actionable insights and the scale of a trusted market infrastructure provider.”

item.title: Tokenisation At An Inflection Point: Dubai Financial Services Authority White Paper Explores The Conditions For Scaling Tokenised Markets
item.content:encoded:
• Scaling Tokenisation: The Road Ahead brings together market perspectives on the custody, digital settlement, interoperability, and cross-border coordination needed for tokenised markets to develop and scale responsibly.

Following its launch at the Future Tokenisation Forum on 5 November, the Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA), the independent banking, financial services, and markets regulator of Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), has published Scaling Tokenisation: The Road Ahead, a white paper examining the conditions that may support the responsible development of tokenised financial assets and related market infrastructure at scale.

The white paper considers tokenisation at an important point of transition from experimentation towards practical use across financial products and market infrastructure. A growing number of tokenised products and infrastructure applications are moving into live use, but adoption remains concentrated in particular asset classes and use cases.

Drawing on structured interviews with practitioners from BlackRock, Ripple, Robinhood, Soter Insure, and Standard Chartered, alongside DFSA expertise and publicly available regulatory, industry, and market research, the white paper highlights areas of broad agreement, differing market views, and practical questions requiring continued discussion across the public and private sectors.

Key highlights

 The white paper identifies five themes that will help shape the next phase of tokenisation:

  • Network effects are bringing significant benefits within reach. The next phase will depend less on the technical feasibility of individual products and more on whether issuers, investors, intermediaries, infrastructure providers, technology firms, and settlement asset providers can connect across a wider ecosystem.
  • Cross-border coordination and common standards will be key enablers. Detailed regulatory harmonisation may not be realistic in the near term, but greater consistency in legal, operational and technical standards can reduce fragmentation and provide clearer conditions for investment and participation.
  • Custody is key to overcoming concerns around safety and security. Issuers and institutional investors are unlikely to deploy tokenisation at scale until they are confident that the associated risks can be appropriately managed. Regulated custody can help institutions manage their exposure.
  • Access to digital cash is a priority. A widely accepted and trusted form of digital cash on-chain is an important prerequisite for tokenisation to deliver benefits, such as simultaneous settlement. Potential settlement models include regulated stablecoins, tokenised commercial bank deposits, and wholesale central bank money.
  • Interoperability will be crucial to achieving scale. Without greater interoperability between blockchains, between trading platforms and between tokenised and traditional market infrastructure, platforms risk becoming isolated “digital islands” that fragment liquidity. Interoperability extends beyond technical connectivity to include workable operational processes, legal certainty, and regulatory coordination across platforms and jurisdictions.

The white paper also notes that tokenisation appears unlikely to pose a material risk to financial stability at its current scale. However, its implications could grow as tokenised markets expand, become more interconnected with traditional finance, and extend across trading, settlement, collateral, and funding markets.

Mark Steward, Chief Executive of the DFSA, said: “Across major international financial centres, the focus is shifting from whether tokenisation can work to how it will work and what needs to change in today’s markets. What stands out from this white paper is that technology alone will not determine the future of tokenisation. Success will also depend on trusted market infrastructure, effective governance and risk management, legal and regulatory certainty, interoperability, commercial viability, and cooperation across the public and private sectors.

No single firm, regulator, or jurisdiction can answer these questions alone. We have brought together perspectives from across the market to support further discussion among industry participants, investors, regulators, policymakers, and international standard-setters.”

The white paper does not prescribe a particular technological, regulatory, or commercial outcome. Instead, it presents a range of market perspectives and highlights questions requiring continued discussion across the public and private sectors.

The full white paper, Scaling Tokenisation: The Road Ahead, is available on the DFSA website.

item.title: Helping Australians Navigate Financial Decisions In An Increasingly Complex Information Environment - Address By ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland At The Ecstra Financial Wellbeing Summit In Sydney On 10 November 2026
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Consumers today have access to more financial information than ever before, however it’s getting harder to know who or what to trust.
  • Building financial capability increasingly involves building digital financial literacy – giving people the ability to distinguish between different information sources, separate truth from hype, and understand the strengths and weaknesses of AI tools.
  • It’s not about putting more information into the system. It’s about understanding what helps people to make better decisions and giving them trusted places to turn.

Good morning.

I’d like to begin by acknowledging the Gadigal people of the Eora nation and by paying respects to elders past and present and I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the room with us today.

When I spoke here last year, I talked about how consumers in the financial system are often vulnerable to exploitation because in almost every decision they make, they’re equipped with less knowledge than the person or the firm on the other side of the transaction.

ASIC’s work in the past year has continued to reinforce this point.

We saw it in our review of mortgage offset accounts, where customers were potentially paying more interest than they should because of banks’ failures to properly set up, monitor or manage offset accounts.

We saw it in our review of car insurance, where customers were in the dark as to why their premiums were rising sharply and repeatedly.

And we saw it in our review of cash settlements in home insurance claims, where many offers were based on quotes from insurers’ preferred suppliers.

Different products, different circumstances, but they underscore the same point:

In a financial system that is becoming harder to navigate, financial wellbeing can’t depend on consumers simply getting better at navigating complexity.

We need to reduce the risk of harm, provide trusted help when people need it, and understand what actually helps people to make better decisions.

And that’s what I’d like to talk to you about today.

The new consumer environment

For a long time, financial capability was largely framed as an ‘information problem’: if people had access to the right information, they’d be better equipped to make good decisions.

I think that everybody in this room recognises that the challenge is more complicated than that.

Consumers today have access to more financial information than ever before. The problem is knowing what and who to trust.

Information comes at consumers from every direction - from social media, targeted advertising, influencers and increasingly AI. And the line between information, marketing and advice is not always obvious.

Scams are becoming increasingly hard to spot.

ASIC is seeing that with the increasing number of pump and dump schemes reported to us, where scammers are often using AI-generated, deep fake videos of well-known personalities and fake news sites to promote investments.

So, a question for all of us to consider is: how do we help people distinguish information that serves them, from information designed to manipulate them?

Adding to the complexity of the issue is the fact that many consumers have a level of anxiety about their financial future and are actively looking for guidance on how they can improve their financial security.

This creates an environment where there is an increased risk of consumer harm, and where we need to work even harder to help people to find their way to information they can trust.

Moneysmart as a trusted source

Moneysmart remains the pre-eminent destination for those seeking trusted financial advice, guidance and resources on a broad range of products and issues.

But in the era of AI, consumers are increasingly not ending up in destinations like Moneysmart but instead are being served AI-generated answers on their phones.

It’s the latest iteration of what has been a changing information landscape since the advent of search engines.

For ASIC, it means doubling down on our strategy of ‘meeting people where they are’, but we are competing with an ecosystem that is pumping out content – some valuable, lots harmful - at scale.

That means that building financial capability increasingly involves building digital financial literacy – the ability to distinguish between different information sources, separate truth from hype, and understand the strengths and weaknesses of AI tools.

It also means working closely with key stakeholders, especially when it comes to assisting consumers who have suffered financial harm.

A current example of this is our work to engage with consumers affected by the Shield and First Guardian collapses which the Minister mentioned earlier.

This is no small task. Over 11,000 people lost money through these collapses – with some having lost their entire retirement savings.

Many only invested after being convinced to move their super by lead generators, who often obtained consumers’ details via social media ads that purported to offer ‘free super reviews’ or ‘super health checks’.

A key goal of our communications has been to encourage those affected to lodge complaints with AFCA because for many, that may be the only pathway to compensation.

At the same time, we have been using every opportunity to warn other consumers how to avoid falling victim to the same harmful lead generation techniques.

While our work is far from done, we have learned some valuable lessons.

There are three in particular that I’d like to call out.

Firstly, we need to communicate harm in ways that reflect consumers’ actual experiences.

In our early communications relating to Shield and First Guardian, we described ‘high pressure sales tactics’ that were being used to convince people to switch their super into high-risk investments.

While our investigations have shown that warning was well-founded, feedback from investors suggested that it didn’t accurately describe what had happened to them.

I’ve listened to many of the call recordings that we’ve gathered in our work and they weren’t overtly high-pressure. They came across as friendly, helpful and informed. They were certainly persuasive but in a gently persistent, rather than pushy, manner.

Adopting different language in our communications has meant that our messages resonate better with those affected, as well as providing better and more effective warnings to others who may be potential victims.

Secondly, steps that seem simple to all of us (like lodging a complaint) can feel complex and overwhelming to consumers - especially those who have experienced a traumatic event.

Back in February, less than 2,000 of the 11,000 investors had lodged a complaint and that number has now doubled to around 4,000.

Through the 14 rounds of emails and direct mail we have sent to various groups of investors, we’ve come to realise that rather than focusing on bombarding people with information on their rights, we need to make taking that first step as simple as possible.

For many Shield and First Guardian investors, the business models were so complex, that they didn’t know who they should lodge a complaint against or for what reason. It was important for us to make the process as easy as possible.

And that brings me to my third insight – that we cannot do it alone, particularly in situations where so many people are affected.

For Shield and First Guardian, we have worked closely with Super Consumers Australia, who have set up a dedicated website that provides simple, easy-to-digest information on what happened, how to make a complaint and how they may be able to get some money back.

Importantly, this includes an easy-to-use, partially pre-filled complaints form that allows people to simply tick boxes in key areas, rather than working out what they need to say.

This is work that is more easily done by a consumer organisation than a regulator, and it’s played an important role in lifting the complaint numbers.

The other thing that we have done through the process is keep in contact with key investor representatives, who have told us what sorts of questions investors need answered, and when our communications were not hitting the mark.

This is not an approach that we can take in response to every fund collapse, but the extraordinary circumstances of Shield and First Guardian required extraordinary responses, and the lessons we’ve learned will be useful in a range of our other financial literacy work.

Getting better at knowing what works

Which leads me to my final point:

We need to get better at understanding what works and we need to find new ways of engaging with consumers.

Over the past year, we’ve completely revamped the Moneysmart website and built a high-quality social media presence.

In the age of AI summaries, we can no longer rely on the old metrics of hits to a website or advertisement reach as a marker of success.

Instead, we need to embrace the harder and more important challenge of changing behaviour, and measuring whether we are succeeding.

That is the key driver behind research we have done with RMIT to develop a financial wellbeing index which we intend to use to measure behavioural change.

And it’s also the reason that ASIC supported Australia's participation in the OECD Adult Financial Literacy Survey – which was informed by the clear support for that step in the room at last year’s summit.

ASIC regards sharing research and insights with the broader financial wellbeing community as an important part of our role, recognising that the goal of building financial capability is shared by people working across government, the community sector and industry.

We’re planning an insight sharing session for early 2027 where we’ll share the results of the OECD survey. If you’d like to know more about the financial wellbeing index or the OECD survey in the meantime, please speak to Jackson Hewett or Andrew Dadswell who are both here today.

Conclusion

If there’s one thought I’d like to leave you with today, it’s this: Financial wellbeing isn’t just about putting more information into the system.

It’s about understanding what helps people to make better decisions, giving them trusted places to turn, and designing a financial system that supports rather than tests their ability to navigate it.

ASIC looks forward to working with all of you to do just that.

item.title: Monetary Authority Of Singapore Launches Central Bank Gold Vaulting Service And Announces Enhanced Tax Framework For Wholesale Gold Activities In Singapore
item.content:encoded:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) announced today the launch of its central bank gold vaulting service, and an enhanced Goods and Services Tax (GST) framework for wholesale investment precious metal (IPM) gold market activities with the Ministry of Finance (MOF). These initiatives mark further progress in Singapore’s efforts to develop as a trusted and efficient gold trading centre serving the Asia-Pacific region.[1]

Launch of MAS Central Bank Gold Vaulting Service

2. MAS has launched its central bank gold vaulting service, providing foreign central banks, international financial institutions[2], and sovereign entities with a secure option to hold gold reserves in Singapore. MAS will also offer gold custody accounts to select Singapore-based bullion banks with expertise and experience in providing gold-related services and trading liquidity to these institutions.

3. Gold will be stored in Singapore’s national currency vault, which can store up to 500 tonnes, with room to expand as demand grows. The service provides an additional sovereign custody option in Singapore, combining secure, allocated custody, reliable servicing and efficient access to gold-market liquidity during Asian trading hours.

Enhanced GST Framework to Support Wholesale Gold Activities in Singapore

4. MAS and MOF will introduce an enhanced GST framework to support wholesale IPM gold market activities in Singapore, which builds on existing GST measures for IPM.[3] It extends the GST waiver to specified wholesale IPM-related services between institutional participants covered by the framework, such as vaulting, refining/recasting, assaying, and broking.

5. This will ensure that the GST treatment better reflects and supports the growth of the wholesale Loco Singapore[4] gold market activities where the gold is not for domestic consumption. The framework is expected to take effect from April 2027, and further details will be announced at Budget 2027.

Looking Ahead: Gold Clearing System Launch in 2027

6. Following the Memorandum of Understanding signed in June, SGX Group and the six founding clearing banks[5] are working closely together to complete preparations for the Over-the-Counter gold clearing system by end-2026. Industry testing of the clearing system has been completed and the clearing system rulebook will be finalised soon. Live trading and market operations are expected to commence in 1Q 2027, with gold market liquidity building throughout the year. Separately, SGX’s physically deliverable Gold Kilobar Futures is targeted for launch in 2Q 2027.

7. Taken together, these initiatives will put in place the key building blocks for a deeper and more vibrant Singapore gold market, facilitate price discovery and risk management during Asian trading hours, while strengthening Singapore’s role as a trusted connector to established gold centres and global liquidity.


***

[1] For further background on Singapore’s initiatives, please refer to: (i) Singapore Sets out Key Focus Areas to Develop Singapore as a Gold Trading Centre  and (ii) Opening Speech by Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong at the 9th Asia-Pacific Precious Metals Conference on 15 June 2026

[2] International financial institutions refer to multilateral organisations established by governments or central banks.

[3] Under the existing Approved Refiner and Consolidator Scheme, GST is waived (i.e. GST is not charged) on IPM-related goods supplied between approved refiners and consolidators for refining activities, to ease their cashflow and compliance. Existing GST measures also exempt the import and local supply of IPM from GST.

[4] Loco Singapore is a gold trading and settlement ecosystem where trades are priced, cleared and settled against gold physically vaulted in Singapore.

[5] The six clearing banks are DBS, Deutsche Bank, ICBC Standard Bank, J.P. Morgan, OCBC, and UOB.

item.title: ASIC Finds Private Credit Practices Continue To Leave Investors In The Dark
item.content:encoded:
Many investors are still not being given the information they need to properly understand the risks, fees and conflicts present in private credit investments as complex structures, opacity and deficient disclosure practices persist, ASIC’s second major surveillance of private credit has found.

Between November 2025 and August 2026, ASIC reviewed 24 wholesale and retail private credit funds responsible for a combined $18 billion in assets under management, as well as a sample of financial advice given to retail investors relating to private credit.

ASIC’s surveillance found that many of the poor fee, disclosure, distribution and conflict-management practices identified in ASIC’s first private credit report, released in November 2025, remain.

The findings, outlined in ASIC’s new report (REP 846), have also led to several regulatory interventions, including six interim stop orders and multiple referrals for further enforcement investigation.

ASIC Commissioner Simone Constant said, ‘Private credit plays a growing role in the Australian economy. The fact that ASIC has issued six interim stop orders since September this year is clear evidence that practices have still not improved in line with this growth.

‘While we have observed pockets of improvement, complexity and opacity persist, in some cases leaving investors unable to properly assess the risks and benefits of their investments. ASIC has made clear what good practice looks like by providing industry with significant guidance, including our ten principles of private credit done well. Our focus now will be on holding the sector accountable for persistent poor practices.

‘Investors should not need forensic skills to understand how a fund operates. They provide the capital and they bear the risk – they are entitled to understand how their money is being used, how risks and conflicts are managed, and whether decisions are made in their interests. When structures get so complex that in some pockets of private credit we have seen more special purpose vehicles within a group than employees to manage investors’ money, effective disclosure of risks to the investors becomes near impossible.’

ASIC's latest surveillance observed:

  • Complex structures and arrangements that masked conflicts and fees, including related-party arrangements, managed in ways that may not have supported fair investor outcomes,
  • Incomplete or inconsistent fee disclosure, including which fees were retained by fund managers, with only two of 22 funds passing on the full economic benefits of interest earned and borrower fees to investors, and
  • Retail distribution practices that failed to clearly communicate risks and support informed decision making, including nine of 12 retail funds failing to clearly explain key information for investor decision making, such as non-performing or distressed assets.

ASIC's surveillance also found that, while most of the financial advice reviewed demonstrated compliance with legal obligations, advisers who recommended higher portfolio concentration to a single private credit fund were less likely to demonstrate compliance with their duty to act in the investor’s best interest. Related party dealings and potential for conflicting interests were, again, warning signs of higher risk of poor conduct and outcomes.

Commissioner Constant continued, ‘Private credit is no longer an asset class confined to institutional investors or high-net-worth individuals. As more Australians are exposed through retail channels and superannuation, strong gatekeepers matter more than ever.

'ASIC is encouraged by some industry efforts to lift practices and develop standards. What matters now is that those standards are adopted and embedded across the sector.

‘It is past time for the sector to embrace its role as good stewards of other people’s money, which means being clear and transparent about risks, fees and conflicts. It is time now for urgent action from all involved in the private credit system.’

ASIC’s surveillance at a glance

Download

  • Report 846: Private Credit Funds: Do investors know what they are getting? (REP 846)

Background

ASIC’s enforcement actions relating to private credit funds

Poor practices in private credit is a 2026 enforcement priority. ASIC has several well-progressed enforcement investigations underway, and this surveillance has resulted in numerous enforcement referrals and interim stop orders, including:

  • Fidante Partners Limited (26-241MR)
  • Australian Secure Capital Fund (26-234MR)
  • Melbourne Securities Corporation Limited (3 stop orders) (26-225MR)
  • Murdoch Clarke Mortgage Management Ltd (26-257MR)

These stop orders were lifted once the issues identified by ASIC were promptly addressed.

ASIC’s private credit focus

ASIC’s private credit work forms part of its multi‑year capital markets roadmap, covering supervision, refreshed regulatory guidance, law reform and enforcement across Australia’s public and private markets (25-264MR).

The roadmap draws on ASIC’s 2025 private credit surveillance (REP 820), which identified gaps in governance, valuation, disclosure, and conflicts management.

In addition to this work, ASIC has:

  • released its ten private credit principles within REP 823,
  • issued a catalogue of key legal obligations for private credit funds (News Item),
  • updated Regulatory Guide 181 AFS licensing: Managing conflicts of interest (RG 181),
  • observed some improvement in private credit fund practices after conducting a voluntary industry survey (News Item), and
  • updated Moneysmart's guidance on private credit to help consumers understand how private credit investments work, which type of investor they suit and what to check before directly investing.

ASIC’s upcoming work in private markets and private credit includes:

  • plans to refresh existing Regulatory Guides for managed funds, to reflect additional requirements in relation to funds with a private credit strategy, and
  • further engagement with industry bodies on stronger standards across retail and wholesale funds. This also encompasses the broader private credit sector, including responsible entities, wholesale trustees, investment managers, distributors, financial advisers, valuers, and auditors.

item.title: Closing Remarks At Roundtable On Machine-Understandable Data In The Age Of Super Intelligence, Paul S. Atkins, SEC Chairman, Washington D.C., Nov. 9, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, and thank you for joining us today for this important discussion on machine-understandable data in the age of super intelligence, or SI.

Before I offer a few closing reflections, I must note that the views I express are my own as Chairman and do not necessarily reflect those of the Commission or of my fellow Commissioner.

Today, we are at the frontier of a new era for financial information and innovation. When I served as an SEC Commissioner two decades ago, many of the machine-understandable disclosures that investors and researchers now take for granted were just beginning to emerge. Financial disclosures designed primarily for people to read are increasingly processed and analyzed by machines. And advances in machine learning and, more recently, generative systems have dramatically expanded the pace and possibilities of financial analysis.

As our DERA staff discussed this morning, the Commission makes 15 data sets available to the public free of cost. In recent years, demand for these resources has grown significantly. In fact, over the past two years, use of the Financial Statement Data Set alone has multiplied more than fivefold. That growth sends a clear message: accessible, standardized data has genuine value.

Lowering the cost of obtaining and analyzing such financial information can empower investors, foster competition, and reduce barriers to entry. Importantly, better data need not mean more disclosure. Often, the greater opportunity lies in making the information that companies already disclose more accessible and useful, without imposing unnecessary burdens on issuers.

Of course, these opportunities must be pursued thoughtfully. SI offers extraordinary potential to improve efficiency and expand access to information. But it does not eliminate the responsibility of issuers to produce, verify, and defend the information that they disclose. The same technologies that can analyze information at unprecedented speed and scale can also magnify errors and missing context. To that end, accuracy and comparability, along with cybersecurity and appropriate oversight, remain essential.

Today's panelists—including technology and data providers, investors, operating companies, practitioners, and academics—offered valuable perspectives on this topic from across our markets. Their insights underscore a fundamental point: even the most sophisticated technology depends on the quality of the information that it uses.

Consider, for example, a high-performance engine. However powerful or finely engineered, it is only as good as the fuel that goes into it. And the same is true of the technologies discussed today: high-quality, well-structured, and trustworthy data is the propellant that allows them to reach their full potential. And while good data cannot eliminate every risk, poor data can undermine even the most sophisticated analytical tools and send our engine sputtering down the road.

That is why this discussion matters. It helps us better understand not only how SI is changing the way that financial information is used, but also how we can encourage innovation while remaining mindful of costs, protecting investors, and preserving market integrity.

As we consider potential next steps, I encourage market participants and other interested parties to continue engaging creatively and thoughtfully with the Commission. Your perspectives will remain invaluable as we work to ensure that our approach to data and SI reflects the practical needs of today’s markets.

In closing, I should like to express my sincere thanks to today’s panelists and moderators for sharing their time and expertise, as well as the dedicated staff of DERA's Office of Data Standards and Innovation for organizing this timely and informative roundtable.

Thank you.

item.title: CFTC Sanctions Eight Individuals For Acting As Unregistered Associated Persons Of Foreign Introducing Brokers
item.content:encoded:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced eight orders filing and settling charges against Michael Talento, Anthony Tyler Williams, Quillan Roberto Black, Christopher Williams, Michael Levi Peters, Jordan Taylor Morgan, Lewis Matthew Neal, and Tyler Evan MacKechnie for acting as unregistered associated persons of unregistered foreign introducing brokers.

According to the orders, the introducing brokers engaged in the solicitation of orders for off-exchange leveraged or margined retail foreign currency and retail commodities transactions with U.S. customers who were not eligible contract participants. The respondents solicited those customers without registering as associated persons of the introducing brokers, as required.

Under the orders, the respondents must cease and desist from engaging in their illegal conduct. They also are barred for two years from registering with the Commission in any capacity or acting as a principal, agent, or employee of any CFTC registrant. Each order also recognizes the penalty the respondent owes in a related Securities and Exchange Commission proceeding.

These orders relate to a prior Commission order sanctioning Netrios LP Ltd. and Red Acre Ltd. for facilitating illegal off-exchange commodity transactions with U.S. customers. [See CFTC Press Release No. 9263-26]

The SEC has filed and settled charges against the respondents based on the same underlying conduct.

item.title: CalPERS’ Climate Solutions Investments Surge To $71 Billion - Pension Giant Also Releases Approach For Responsibly Investing In Artificial Intelligence
item.content:encoded:
CalPERS announced Monday that its investments in climate solutions had grown to reach $71 billion as of June 30, 2026. The new figure represents an increase of $11 billion since last year, and $24 billion since the strategy initially launched in November of 2023.

“The strong and steady growth means CalPERS remains on track to meet our goal of capitalizing on the transition to a low-carbon economy by investing $100 billion by 2030 in climate solutions as part of our Climate Action Plan,” said CalPERS Chief Executive Officer Marcie Frost. “CalPERS remains committed to finding opportunities in climate solutions to help power future generations and provide the pension benefits that our members have earned.”

The Climate Action Plan outlines a global strategy to generate strong performance on behalf of CalPERS members by investing in opportunities created by the ongoing shift to a low-carbon economy.

“Money from around the world continues to pour into the climate market, with $2.3 trillion invested in energy transition and clean technology projects in 2025,” said CalPERS Chief Investment Officer Stephen Gilmore. “Renewable energy is cleaner, cheaper and faster to bring to market than conventional power sources, and CalPERS is providing the capital necessary to meet those needs.”

Investments include those that support increased electricity generation, improved power grid efficiency, and utilities seeking to transition from fossil fuel-based energy sources to renewable ones. CalPERS also invests in climate solutions that reduce the threat that pollution and rising global temperatures pose to the overall health of the pension fund. The increase to $71 billion is a result of new investments and the appreciation of existing investments.

“Investing in climate solutions is increasingly important because global temperatures continue to rise around us, which can impact the financial performance of the portfolio.” said CalPERS Managing Investment Director of Sustainable Investing Peter Cashion. “Since the physical climate risk is likely to grow across our portfolio, our targets include investments that make assets, communities, and supply chains more resilient to a changing world.”

Responsible AI Approach

CalPERS also announced it will present its Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) approach at its upcoming board meeting on November 16. The framework looks at AI through the lens of risk management, as well as value creation and preservation.

“This is one of our top priorities, and CalPERS is working with its partners on how AI projects use energy and water, as well as the impact they have on a community,” Frost said. “The AI buildout has moved so quickly, and a key part going forward is to ensure that these investments are done in a sustainable way.”

In April, CalPERS updated its proxy voting guidelines to include that directors could be held accountable for failing to oversee AI risk. The issue of AI was also a topic of discussion in more than 100 company engagements during the 2026 proxy season. On the private side, CalPERS is beginning to incorporate Responsible AI in its diligence program and is also actively taking part in industry efforts to promote consistent expectations on AI oversight and disclosure.

“Effective AI policies and governance processes are important for the performance, stability, and resiliency of the market and the long-term performance of our portfolio,” Gilmore said. “We will engage policy makers and support policies that promote transparency in AI application and decision-making.”

item.title: Opening Remarks At The Roundtable On Machine-Understandable Data In The Age Of Super Intelligence, SEC Commissioner Mark T. Uyeda, Washington D.C., Nov. 9, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome to today’s roundtable on machine‑understandable data and super intelligence. Thank you to everyone who is here in person and to those who are joining online. I regret that I cannot be with you in person, but I appreciate the opportunity to share a few thoughts.

The Commission’s disclosure-based regime rests on the premise that investors and markets make better decisions when companies provide timely, accurate, honest and financially material information. For much of our history, the reader of disclosures was a person with a printed document. Then it was an analyst with a screen. Today, increasingly, the first reader of a filing is a machine. Whether it is a quantitative model, a large language model, or other super-intelligence tool, these machines extract, ingest, and interpret disclosures at a speed and scale that humans cannot match. As super-intelligence tools become more widely used, that trend will only accelerate.

So, how can machine-readable data complement super intelligence? Does a format that was introduced over two decades ago still have value in an SI environment?

The Commission mandated XBRL starting in 2009,[1] and we have since required Inline XBRL[2] and expanded structured data requirements to additional filings.[3] While these requirements carry compliance costs that we as regulators should be mindful of, they have also led to significant benefits. Structured data is critical to attracting research analyst coverage, especially for smaller companies, even when that coverage is automated or aggregated in large databases. In other words, machine-readable data can increase visibility, which in turn lowers the cost of capital by making information easier to find, compare, and analyze for investors. 

Super intelligence, far from making XBRL irrelevant, may make this connection even stronger as machine-readable data can feed the SI tools with more reliable and consistent data inputs. SI tools can potentially analyze smaller companies that were historically overlooked or spot patterns and trends in data in ways that prior technology did not. The technology is advancing so quickly that none of us can say what these tools will be capable of in a few years. 

Today’s discussion is a valuable step in thinking about how SEC filing data can be better utilized in the age of super intelligence, including whether there are new methods that are superior to XBRL. The first panel will explore how market participants are currently using these tools. The second panel will examine the risks and costs the Commission should consider and how we might better facilitate progress. I encourage everyone to be candid, including about where the Commission can do better. Facilitating capital formation is part of our tripartite mission, and high-quality structured data can help advance it.

I want to thank Dr. Joshua White, Julie Marlowe, Valerie Szczepanik, and the staff of the Division of Economic Risk Analysis who organized this event, as well as our panelists for sharing their time and expertise. Thank you.

item.title: Central Bank Independence In Today’s World - Speech By Andrew Bailey, Governor, Bank Of England, Given At The SIAF Lecture Series, Zurich University
item.content:encoded:
In this speech Andrew Bailey argues that today’s shock prone world makes independent and accountable central banks more important than ever, both to control inflation and safeguard financial stability. Andrew is also optimistic about the potential benefits of AI to productivity and sustainable economic growth, but also outlines the financial stability risks posed by AI.

Andrew Bailey

Governor, Bank of England

Speech

It is a great pleasure to be here in Zurich.

The main focus this evening is to have a discussion. I am just going to make a few opening comments across the subjects of central bank independence, financial stability and technology – as a prompt to get our discussion going.

We are living through difficult times. Imagine if any of us had been asked ten years ago what were the odds of major military conflicts in Europe and the Middle East at the same time. The economics of these events are supply shocks – which tend to push prices and inflation up and activity down at the same time. Such shocks are challenging for central banks, and particularly when they are large and more frequent. A shock prone world is more difficult.

At the same time, we are seeing growing signs of the beginnings of a positive supply shock coming from AI and the investment required for that. In the UK, economic activity is turning out to be more resilient than we had expected, and some of that is due to AI investment, particularly in the business services sector.

These are challenging times for independent central banks setting monetary policy and for the people we serve. These shocks push inflation away from our targets – our definitions of price stability. Our task is to set interest rates to bring inflation back to target. I do recognise that in Switzerland you have experienced a record of more subdued inflation.

When it comes to the independence of central banks, I would say two things. Yes, these conditions are more challenging. But, it is in the challenging times that we need robust institutions more than ever.

There is though an important further step in this line of argument, which may seem obvious but needs stating. As independent institutions, we are not independent of the people of our countries. We serve them and are accountable to them. This is our public legitimacy. And by this I mean the whole people. I think our independence and legitimacy depends on this – we don’t and shouldn’t select those whom we serve and we are therefore inherently plural in our approach to our societies. This is a critical feature of independence.

Let me turn now to financial stability and central bank independence. Monetary and financial stability are in my view inseparable as the core principles of central banks. They are both equally and firmly anchored around the stability of the value of money. But, notwithstanding this in my experience, the political economy of independence is different. When it comes to monetary policy, while there can be debate around the form and precise structure of the arrangements, the independence of the actual decisions on interest rates is not in doubt. But this does not carry over to financial stability, where the decisions are much more contested. The lobbying moreover is much louder, and the interests much more sharply defined I would argue.

This is illustrated by the current state of affairs. Memories of the financial crisis are receding. But it is contributing to pressure to ease back regulation. I don’t pretend that every one of our rules and regulations in the UK is perfect.

But, I do contend that sustained economic growth depends on financial stability. So, it matters. It also matters that so far we have come through the latest adverse economic shocks with a resilient financial system. That’s not an accident. The post crisis regulatory reforms have made a difference here. And, the final “it matters”, we are seeing the risks shift into new areas of the financial landscape.

Which brings me to my last subject – technology, and particularly AI. I am an optimist on AI, digital technology and most probably robotics too. They have the potential to lift the sustainable growth rates of many economies through raising productivity growth. That is a good thing.

But with that do come risks, the risks of how to come to terms with AI for instance. In our world, Frontier AI has increased the risk from cyber-attacks – something that was already prominent. More broadly, it has led to concerns which may call into question public trust in AI. This is critical. We must act promptly to identify ways to give the public the level of trust they want and deserve. To achieve this, we must be clear what public interest objectives we are pursuing and how we achieve them. A clear case for me is that we need more extensive model testing, pre and post release. This may lead us to conclude that we want more or different points or means of human user intervention in the operation of AI. We also certainly want better incident reporting, monitoring and follow up (to make sure we learn the lessons from them). The key point is that public trust will depend on assured human intervention. AI will succeed as a tool of humans.

Why does this matter for central banks you may well ask? It matters a lot I would argue. Let me briefly set out two reasons for this, which are closely interconnected, and linked to financial stability.

Throughout modern history there has been a close relationship between economic growth, the interest of businesses in fuelling that growth, and the public interest as defined and represented by governments and in some areas of public policy put into effect by institutions such as central banks. You don’t need to take any ideological position to believe in this nexus of connections – you could be Hayek, Keynes, Marx or Schumpeter.

The question we face today is whether AI poses a new and more forceful challenge to the nexus, in the sense that the risk of a loss of public trust requires a careful but determined response to underpin that trust and support the economic growth that we all want to see? My response to this question would be yes it does pose such a challenge. Put simply, if you say “very good things can come from this, but bad things may happen too”, you can’t leave it there. And, it deepens the dependency between commercial success and public policy.

But second, and finally, there is a powerful connection to financial stability here. There is a lot of speculation on the subject of whether there is an asset price bubble in AI, and the financial stability risks that go with that. Bubble spotting is an imprecise science. But, let’s recognise that such a risk exists, which we should do. How might the bubble burst and potentially cause a problem? Four arguments can I think be advanced here.

First, it is the job of financial markets to value uncertain future returns. The returns from AI may be good, but still markets may overvalue them. That’s in the nature of the task of valuing uncertainty.

Second, the returns may be good, and they may match expectations, but they take longer to be realised than predicted. This has been the case historically with big General Purpose Technology innovation – take Edison and electricity for instance. There are good reasons to believe that the world moves faster now, but still the timing may not live up to market expectations.

Third, everyone is priced to be a winner, but history tends to tell us that this is not the case. Remember Netscape.

Fourth, the public trust point – there is a certain fragility created by this nexus. Arguably it is not new. A British Prime Minister was killed by one of the earliest steam locomotives, people worried about the dangers of electricity. I would argue that at present the argument seems more powerful with AI – but as I noted earlier, I treat that as a problem to be solved. But, until we have done so it could affect asset valuations.

So, there are clear financial stability risks here, and that’s without talking explicitly about cyber risks.

I said I would use my opening remarks to stir up some questions. Let’s see!

I would like to thank Sarah Breeden, Karen Jude, Clare Lombardelli, Dave Ramsden and James Talbot for their assistance in preparing these remarks.

item.title: The EBA Streamlines The 2027 EU-Wide Stress Test With More Than 55% Reduction In Requested Data
item.content:encoded:
The European Banking Authority (EBA) today released the final methodology, draft templates, and template guidance for its 2027 EU-wide stress test, together with the key milestones for the exercise. Following extensive engagement with industry participants, the EBA has significantly streamlined the exercise, reducing the number of required data points by 55% through the simplification of reporting templates and closer alignment with supervisory reporting. These changes will reduce operational burden and improve efficiency while preserving the robustness, risk-sensitivity and comparability of stress test results. The 2027 exercise will also include, for the first time, a dedicated module assessing climate-related risks. The 2027 EU-wide stress test will formally start in January 2027, following the release of the macroeconomic and climate scenarios, with the results scheduled for publication by the end of July 2027.

The 2027 EU-wide stress test will continue to follow a constrained bottom-up approach, complemented by top-down elements, and based on a static balance sheet assumption. It will assess the impact of adverse shocks on banks’ solvency across key risk areas and income streams under both baseline and adverse scenarios. The methodology also defines the sample of participating banks for the 2027 EU-wide stress test, although the sample may be subject to changes ahead of the launch of the exercise.

Compared with the previous exercise, the number of required data points has been reduced by 55%, mainly by streamlining the templates and relying more closely on regular supervisory reporting concepts, particularly in credit risk. These improvements are expected to reduce reporting burden and improve data quality and consistency.

For the first time, physical and transition climate risks will be assessed through a dedicated module, without affecting the core stress test results.

The draft stress test templates and guidance published today may be subject to minor technical adjustments before the formal launch of the exercise.

Key Milestones for the 2027 EU-wide Stress Test
  • Launch of the exercise: end of January 2027
  • First submission of results to the EBA: end of April 2027
  • Second submission to the EBA: end of May 2027
  • Final submission to the EBA: early July 2027
  • Publication of results: end of July 2027

Note to the editors

  • The simplification of the 2027 stress test templates and methodology is part of the forthcoming supervisory reporting changes announced on 10 April 2026.
  • The 2027 EU-wide stress test methodological package marks another important milestone under the EBA’s communication campaign “Simplifying to strengthen: building a more efficient EU prudential and supervisory framework”. This initiative is part of the EBA’s broader priority to simplify and enhance the efficiency of the regulatory and supervisory framework, in line with the work of its Task Force on Efficiency (TFE) and the EBA’s Report on the efficiency of the regulatory and supervisory framework, published on 1 October 2025. The proposed changes aim to reduce unnecessary operational burden while preserving a robust, consistent and risk-sensitive framework across the EU banking sector.
  • The aim of the EU-wide stress test is to assess the resilience of EU banks to a common set of adverse economic developments, identifying potential risks (including environmental ones), informing supervisory decisions, and increasing market discipline.
  • The EBA conducts the stress test in a bottom-up fashion with some top-down elements, using consistent methodologies, scenarios, and key assumptions developed jointly with other authorities.
  • The exercise is coordinated by the EBA in cooperation with the European Central Bank, the European Systemic Risk Board, and the Competent Authorities from all relevant national jurisdictions.
  • To give banks sufficient time to prepare, the EBA published the methodology and templates (including scenario templates) well ahead of the formal launch by end of January 2027, when the relevant macroeconomic scenarios will be released.

item.title: Machine-Understandable Data In The Age Of Super Intelligence, Joshua White, Chief Economist And Director, SEC Division Of Economic And Risk Analysis, Washington D.C., Nov. 9, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Good morning and thank you for joining us today. I am Josh White, Director of the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis, or DERA.

Before I begin, let me offer our standard disclaimer on behalf of all of today’s SEC participants. Our remarks are provided in our official capacities as Commission staff but do not necessarily reflect the views of the Commission, the Commissioners, or other members of the staff.

We are here today because something fundamental is changing in how financial information is used in our markets.

Investors have long relied on financial disclosures to make informed decisions: reading filings and studying tables. Increasingly, they also use databases, analytical systems, and superintelligence models to help them access and analyze that information.

However, while tools are changing, the purpose of disclosure remains the same: to provide investors with material information to inform their decisions. And this purpose leads me to the focus of today’s event: How disclosed information is organized, accessed, and used; and where structured formats offer benefits that justify their costs. As you will hear shortly, downloads of the SEC’s structured datasets have increased dramatically over the past year. That is a striking change and one that makes understanding how these data are being used especially important.

It also brings us to the topic at the heart of today’s discussion: making information machine-readable may not be the same as making it machine-understandable. The question is not simply whether a system can extract a number from a filing. It is whether that system can identify what the number represents, interpret it in context, and compare it appropriately.

With that in mind, I would like to frame today’s conversation around three questions.

First, what are the benefits? We want to understand whether and how structured data help investors make faster, better-informed decisions, reduce the cost of analysis, and improve the allocation of capital. We are also interested in how these data can help regulators and economists understand market dynamics, and how advances in superintelligence are changing the ways you use structured and unstructured data.

Second, what are the costs and risks? Reliable data require resources to produce, validate, and use. We want to understand where those costs are greatest and where there are opportunities to reduce them. That includes exploring whether superintelligence can help issuers prepare structured disclosures more efficiently while improving their quality. It also means understanding where the same disclosed information can be used effectively without a structured format, and whether the benefits of structuring it justify the associated costs. We want to hear about the risks that arise when automated systems rely on information that is inaccurate, inconsistent, or missing important context, and how those risks can be addressed.

Third, what is working in practice and what is not? We want to hear concrete examples where structured disclosed information is most useful, where it adds less value, and why. That includes your experience with financial statement disclosures and other types of structured information. We also welcome your perspectives on the quality and usability of these data, and on what changes, if any, the SEC should consider.

As analytical tools become more capable, our focus should remain on the investors those tools serve. Reliable information and the context needed to interpret it remain essential.

Our goal today is to better understand when structuring disclosed information makes it more useful, and how to achieve those benefits efficiently.

Thus, the central question before us is how structured formats can best support the use of disclosed financial information, with careful attention to both benefits and costs. Your experience and insights are essential to answering that question. We want to understand not just what the technology promises, but what it delivers: the benefits you are realizing, the costs you are bearing, and the problems that remain. Those insights will help inform how the SEC approaches the format and usability of disclosed information as technology and market practices evolve.

Thank you for being here and sharing your perspectives. I look forward to the conversation ahead.

item.title: Cboe Expands Prediction Markets Suite To Small-Caps With Launch Of Mini-Russell 2000 Index Binary Options
item.content:encoded:
Cboe Global Markets, Inc. (Cboe: CBOE), a leading global markets operator and pioneer in equity and index derivatives, today announced the launch of mini-Russell 2000 Index (MRUT) binary options (ticker: MRTBW). The binary options based on MRUT, which is 1/10th the size of the Russell 2000 Index, began trading on November 9 and are the latest addition to Cboe's prediction market suite.

MRTBW are yes or no directional trades that pay $100 or $0, depending on whether the MRUT settles at, above or below the specified level. For example, an investor who makes a trade that MRUT will close above 280 will receive $100 at settlement if it closes at 280 or above, while the contract will pay $0 if the index closes below 280. Cboe will list P.M.-settled contracts expiring on the same and next trading day, and MRTBW options offerings are centrally cleared through the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC).

"Small-cap stocks are closely watched by retail investors and can play an important role in a portfolio, and Cboe's new MRUT binary options allow investors to make yes-or-no trades on a leading small-cap index," said JJ Kinahan, Head of Retail Expansion and Alternative Investment Products at Cboe. "The Russell 2000 Index is traditionally more volatile than other broad measures, which is part of why demand for zero-days-to-expiry options tied to the index has grown significantly in recent years. As interest in short-dated exposure grows, Cboe continues to expand its SEC-regulated prediction markets offerings and provide investors with the ability to trade and learn more about market outcomes within the safeguards of the securities markets."

"The Russell 2000 Index is the leading benchmark for the U.S. small-cap equity market, providing investors with a trusted and objective measure of this important market," said Shawn Creighton, Director of Index Derivatives Solutions at FTSE Russell. "Our longstanding partnership with Cboe has been instrumental in expanding access to innovative index-based products, and this latest development builds on that relationship by giving investors more ways to access U.S. small caps and manage risk."

The Russell 2000 Index measures the performance of the small-cap segment of the U.S. equity market. The index includes approximately 2,000 of the smallest companies based on a combination of their market capitalization and current index membership. The Russell 2000 Index is a subset of the Russell 3000 Index, which is designed to represent approximately 98% of the investible U.S. equity market. Cboe has seen record demand in its traditional Russell 2000 Index (RUT) options suite, with average daily volume of 85 thousand contracts through the first three quarters.   

With the launch of MRUT binary options, Cboe's prediction markets suite now includes the ability to trade outcomes tied to small-cap and large-cap (S&P 500 Index) equities and will soon include certain SEC-regulated corporate earnings metrics. Cboe's prediction markets offerings are available through select retail brokers and leverage the protections of the U.S. registered securities trading environment.

To learn more about Cboe's offerings, visit Cboe Prediction Markets.

item.title: ICE Mortgage Monitor: 2.4 Million Mortgage Holders Are Equity Millionaires As Q3 Home Equity Hits Record High - Servicer Retention Declined In Q3, With Cash-Out Refinances Accounting For 75% Of Refinance Portfolio Attrition
item.content:encoded:
Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), one of the world’s leading providers of financial market technology and data powering global capital markets, today released the November 2026 ICE Mortgage Monitor Report. The analysis finds that home equity and the number of equity millionaires both reached record third-quarter highs, creating opportunities for lenders and servicers to engage borrowers seeking access to that wealth.

“Homeowners are sitting on substantial housing wealth, with 2.4 million mortgage holders now holding at least $1 million in equity,” said Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at ICE. “In a higher rate environment, cash-outs are making up a greater share of refinances, with those homeowners giving up historically low mortgage rates and taking on higher monthly payments to tap into their equity.”

Key findings from the November ICE Mortgage Monitor include:

  • Home equity reached a record third-quarter high
    Mortgage holders collectively held $17.5 trillion in equity in Q3, up 1.4% year over year. Tappable equity that can be accessed while maintaining a 20% cushion rose 1.2% to an average of $204,000 per borrower, an increase of $16,600 from a year ago.
  • The number of equity millionaires reached a Q3 record
    2.4 million mortgage holders had at least $1 million in equity, up 6% year over year, while nearly 9 million held $500,000 or more, up 4%. California accounted for 49% of the nation’s equity millionaires, followed by New York (189,000), New Jersey (141,000) and Florida (104,000).
  • Rising rates drove increased share of cash-out refinances
    Cash-out transactions accounted for 1 in 7 rate locks in recent weeks, and purchase loans accounted for roughly 80% of rate locks.
  • ARMs remained popular due to higher rates and more attractive spreads
    Adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) accounted for more than 10% of early October rate locks as 30-year fixed rates moved above 7%. The points-adjusted spread between 5/1 ARMs and 30-year fixed loans widened from roughly 75 basis points over the summer to more than 100 basis points in early October, further increasing the attractiveness of ARMs.
  • Refinance retention declined as cash-out activity grew
    Servicers retained 27% of refinancing borrowers, down four percentage points from the prior quarter, while retention among rate-and-term refinancers fell nine percentage points to 30%. Cash-out retention held at 26%, with servicers retaining just 15% of cash-out borrowers who took out loans in 2019 or earlier. Cash-out refinances accounted for 75% of all refinance-portfolio attrition.

“Traditional rate-based retention strategies aren’t effective for borrowers who are motivated by access to equity rather than interest rate savings,” said Bob Hart, President of Mortgage Technology at ICE. “To retain these borrowers, servicers need better visibility into their equity positions and the ability to engage them before they look elsewhere. By combining ICE’s retention analytics with connected technologies like MSP, Servicing Digital and Encompass, we’re helping lenders and servicers identify opportunities, connect borrowers with financing options and keep those relationships intact.”

Further detail on home equity, servicer retention, home price, and mortgage performance trends — including charts — can be found in the full ICE Mortgage Monitor report at https://mortgagetech.ice.com/resources/data-reports.
